text: Install Graft and check what it needs. Each of the five steps to installing an app has its own page.

Download Graft.zip from GitHub Releases. On an Intel Mac, download Graft-Intel.zip instead (a test build; see Requirements). Unzip it, move Graft.app to /Applications, and open it. Graft.app carries everything it needs: the graft CLI, with its own Python; cyan, zsign, ldid, ipatool, UnfairPlay and the other helpers. You don't need Homebrew, pipx, Python, Go, Xcode or libimobiledevice. The one exception is decrypting on a jailbroken device, which still needs libimobiledevice's iproxy and tools you install yourself (see Decrypt on a jailbroken device).

A Mac with macOS 14 or later, or macOS 13 or later for the Intel download. On a Mac with Apple silicon, download Graft.zip, which does everything. On an Intel Mac, download Graft-Intel.zip, which also runs on macOS 13. It's a test build until it has run on a real Intel Mac. Everything works except what needs Apple silicon: App Store sign-in, and getting and decrypting App Store apps, older versions and free ones included (search still works, for adding an app by name, and needs no sign-in); Set Up Decryption; Build for this Mac, and handing builds to PlayCover. Those buttons are there but disabled, with "Needs a Mac with Apple silicon", and Settings › App Store says so in one line, with no sign-in or setup to do. Use a decrypted IPA you already have, or dump one from a jailbroken device. Graft.zip opened on an Intel Mac only says to download Graft-Intel.zip; Graft-Intel.zip on an Apple silicon Mac runs, with a banner saying to download Graft.zip for everything. An iPhone or iPad paired with this Mac, connected by USB, or on the same network with Wi-Fi sync turned on. An Apple account, of one of two kinds. The first run asks which you have, and Settings switches later. A free Apple ID, with LiveContainer on the device. Graft builds unsigned IPAs and pushes them into LiveContainer, which signs them when you import them. Graft never signs anything itself on this account. A paid Apple Developer Program membership, with a development certificate exported as a .p12 and a provisioning profile (a wildcard profile is simplest) that includes your device.

To You need Build and push into LiveContainer LiveContainer on the device. With a free Apple ID, install it with SideStore, AltStore, iloader or Impactor, which also refresh it every 7 days. Install an app as a normal app (Sideload) A paid membership, its .p12 and a profile that includes the device. Install or update LiveContainer from Graft A paid membership and an App Store Connect API key. Make each app's provisioning profile automatically A paid membership and an App Store Connect API key. Search the App Store Nothing. No Apple ID is involved. Download from the App Store A Mac with Apple silicon, and an Apple ID signed in in Graft. Any Apple ID works, free or paid; it's separate from the account above. The app must be one that Apple ID owns, or a free one Graft can get for it. Decrypt App Store downloads A Mac with Apple silicon, and an iPhone or iPad app installed on it from the Mac App Store, with the same Apple ID, and opened once. Any free one will do. Decrypt on a jailbroken device A jailbroken iPhone or iPad with frida-server 16.x and OpenSSH, plus tools you install yourself (see Decrypt on a jailbroken device). Run a build on this Mac A Mac with Apple silicon, and PlayCover, a free app you install yourself. Graft doesn't include it.

Each step has its own page: Set up your Apple account Add an app Give it a decrypted IPA Attach tweaks Build and install After that, Graft checks your apps for updates at launch and once a day while it's open. An app with something to update shows an arrow mark in the sidebar; see Updating your apps.
Graft works with a free Apple ID or a paid Apple Developer account, and Settings can switch between the two later. The first time it opens, Graft asks "Do you have a paid Apple Developer account?"

No, I have a free Apple ID. That's all on the Mac. Graft lists the steps to do on the iPhone or iPad, with your free Apple ID: Install SideStore, or use iloader. Install LiveContainer (guide). The LiveContainer+SideStore build uses one app slot for both. In LiveContainer, open Settings and tap Import Certificate from SideStore, so it can sign the apps you import. iloader doesn't do this for you, and on iOS 26 every app fails its first launch with "JITLess mode is required since iOS 26" until it's done. Graft finds LiveContainer on the device by its bundle id, so there is no team id to set up.

Yes. Choose your .p12. Type its password (leave it empty if you set none). Choose your provisioning profile. Graft shows the team and the devices the profile covers before it sets anything up. It keeps the password in your login keychain, never in a file, and copies both files into its config folder.

The Account row in Settings switches between the two, with Add a paid account… or Switch to a free Apple ID…, and keeps your apps, repos and settings either way. With a paid account, Replace certificate and profile… swaps in a new pair when the old one expires, which happens every year.

Add an app to Graft by searching the App Store, or from its App Store URL or a name and bundle id. Press + at the top of the sidebar. Add App opens on Search. Type an app's name, and pick it from the results. Choose its delivery, and press Add. You can also paste its App Store URL, or fill in a name and bundle id by hand.
Add App (+ at the top of the sidebar) has three ways in.

Search is the default. Type an app's name, and the App Store's iPhone apps that match appear as you type, each with its icon, developer and price. Results come from the store in the sheet's Store picker. It starts at this Mac's region (System Settings › General › Language & Region). A territory such as Puerto Rico or Réunion uses the store its people shop in (US, France), and a region with no App Store uses the US store and says so. Pick one with the mouse or the arrow keys, choose its delivery, and press Add (or Return). That adds it exactly as its App Store URL would. A paid app shows its price, and a listing that gives none says "Price unknown", never "Free". A result already in your config says so, and names the app it was added as. Apple's own apps can be found but not got: iOS ships them, and only Apple can sign them. Apple limits how often one Mac can search. A term you already searched while the sheet is open is answered from memory, and if Apple does say no, the sheet says to try again shortly.
Paste the app's apps.apple.com link.
A name and a bundle id, and optionally an IPA you already have.

section: Which store an app is looked up in
text: Graft remembers the store an app came from (store_country in config.yaml), and checks its updates, its icon and its price there. Edit App shows it under App Store and can change it. An app added from a URL keeps the store the URL names (apps.apple.com/gb/..., or the older itunes.apple.com/gb/...). An app with no store (from a URL that names none, or added by hand) is looked up in the store of this Mac's region, then in the US store. The first that sells it answers, and nothing is written. When neither has it, the error names both stores. A hand-written store_country that isn't an App Store is ignored, with a warning; UK is read as GB.

A build needs a decrypted IPA of the app. There are three ways to get one. From the App Store. Once you've signed in and set up decryption (see App Store Downloads), the app's Source IPA section has Get latest from App Store. Graft downloads the app, decrypts it on this Mac, and stages it. If that version is already staged, by Get latest, a drop or a dump, it says "Already have <version>" and downloads nothing; Get Again downloads it anyway. Get an older version… beside it gets one of the app's earlier versions instead (see Get an older version). An IPA you already have. Drop it on the app's pane. A dump from your own jailbroken device, from the device's Decrypt card. See Decrypt on a jailbroken device. These are for personal use: your own Apple ID, apps you own or get for free, on your own devices. Don't redistribute decrypted or modified IPAs.

Each way stages the IPA in ~/.cache/graft/ipas/, and a build uses it from there. Graft checks every Mach-O binary in it before injecting and warns if any is still encrypted; the build carries on, but the app will most likely not launch. With nothing staged, the build stops and lists the ways to get one. The App Store route has its own page, App Store Downloads.

Drop the IPA on the app's pane, or choose it in Add App's Manual mode. Graft checks that the IPA's bundle id matches the app's and stages it under its canonical name. An IPA that is still encrypted (straight from the App Store) is decrypted with UnfairPlay on the way in if decryption is set up, and refused if it isn't.

The device's Decrypt card dumps an installed app off your own jailbroken iPhone or iPad, and Add as app turns the dump into an app. This path needs tools Graft.app doesn't include, which you install yourself: Tool Used for frida 16.x on the device Both backends. The device's frida-server must be 16.x, the major frida-ios-dump's virtualenv installs. Graft has no frida of its own: it asks frida-ios-dump's (graft_ipa/frida_probe.py), so until frida-ios-dump is set up, the decrypt check can't reach frida-server and says so. frida-ios-dump One backend. Clone it to ~/.local/share/graft/frida-ios-dump, check out 56e99b2 (its last release for frida 16; the current one needs frida 17), and create a .venv there with pip install 'frida==16.*' paramiko scp tqdm, or set GRAFT_FRIDA_IOS_DUMP. The decrypt check prints these commands when it isn't set up. Needs OpenSSH on the device. bagbak The other backend. npm install -g bagbak@4.0.3 for a 16.x frida-server. iproxy, from libimobiledevice The SSH tunnel to the device. brew install libimobiledevice, or from MacPorts, sudo port install libimobiledevice. The card checks what, if anything, is blocking a dump right now. On a device with no jailbreak it says so in one line, and Dump in the device's list of apps waits. Unless you choose a backend, Graft picks the one that can run, preferring frida-ios-dump: frida-ios-dump attaches to the running app. Graft brings it to the foreground first, launching it if needed. It copies the bundle over SSH: store the device's root password with Set root password…, or set GRAFT_SSH_KEY (and GRAFT_SSH_USER if it isn't root). bagbak spawns the app itself. bagbak 4.x (the version that works with a 16.x frida-server) also copies the bundle over SSH, using the same stored root password; it can't use GRAFT_SSH_KEY. A dump is always of the whole app, which is what gets verified and staged. A dump that leaves app extensions encrypted (an extension built for a newer iOS than the device runs) drops them and stages the rest, and says what it removed. The app keeps working, minus those widgets and share extensions.

Cache lists every staged IPA, and marks the one a build uses when a bundle id has more than one. From there you can add a dump as an app, install it on this Mac with PlayCover, or delete it. Staged IPAs are never pruned.

Once you've signed in and set up decryption, Graft downloads and decrypts the apps your Apple ID owns or can get for free. Graft downloads the App Store's IPA with ipatool and decrypts it with UnfairPlay, both inside Graft.app. It only downloads apps your Apple ID already owns, or free ones it gets for that Apple ID; a paid app is bought in the App Store, never by Graft. Everything happens on your own Mac, for your own devices. There are two one-time steps, both in Settings › App Store: Sign in and Set up decryption. Settings is the last item in the sidebar, under Activity: Graft has no separate Settings window, so ⌘, opens nothing.

Press Sign In…. Type your Apple ID (email or phone) and password. Type the 6-digit code if Apple asks for one (it doesn't always). About signing in: Graft types your Apple ID, password and code into the bundled ipatool's own prompts. They go only to Apple, through that ipatool. Graft never saves them, and never puts them on a command line, in the environment or in a log. ipatool, which comes with Graft, keeps your sign-in, including your password, in your login Keychain, as it does when you use it on its own. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's App Store components (about 320 MB) and its Unicorn emulator, and can take several minutes. Later ones take under a minute. See What Graft Downloads. If you signed in with your own ipatool, the sheet says so first: signing in here removes that sign-in, and your own ipatool will need to sign in again if you still use it in Terminal. While you're signed in, Sign In Again… sits beside Sign Out. Use it when Apple has ended the session: a get then says so, and names the button. Sign Out signs ipatool out.

Install any free iPhone or iPad app from the Mac App Store (only an Apple silicon Mac can), signed in there with the same Apple ID you use in Graft, and open it once. Press Set Up Decryption…. In the sheet, pick that app (the first one is already picked) and press Set Up Decryption… again. Graft then explains what will happen. Open the app once first (the sheet's Open <app> button does it): macOS sometimes clears the App Store state UnfairPlay reads, and opening the app writes it again. Then press Continue. macOS's dialog usually names Graft and asks you to allow it administrator access ("Allow administrator access for “Graft”?"). On a Mac with Touch ID it offers Touch ID or Use Password…; on one without, it asks for your password. If Graft has to start this step through osascript instead, the dialog names osascript. Cancel stops here. Graft never sees the password. If your macOS account isn't an administrator, macOS's dialog asks for an administrator's name and password instead, so someone who administers this Mac has to type them. The rest is the same: Graft never sees them, and the decryption model it sets up is yours. What happens: Before root copies anything, it checks that this Mac's App Store state (SC Info.sidb) is there. If it isn't, the step stops at once, nothing is changed, and Graft says which app to open. Graft explains the step before macOS's dialog appears, and shows the exact command under "The exact command, run as root". Root works only in a folder of its own, on its own copy of the app, and runs its own copy of UnfairPlay. In a Graft.app signed with a developer team, as releases are, root checks that copy against Graft.app's team before it runs it, and when Graft.app is signed with Developer ID, the copy must be too. A copy nothing can check is shown as a warning, and runs only if you press "Run Unchecked Copy as Root…". UnfairPlay saves a private decryption model, which Graft then moves into your own folder, as you. Cancel is always safe. The step also stops by itself if it runs far longer than expected (15 minutes for most apps, longer for a very large one). Decryption then works only for apps downloaded with that Apple ID. If you switch Apple ID, in Graft or in the Mac App Store, press Set Up Again… with an app installed under the new one.

On the app's pane, Get latest from App Store downloads, decrypts and stages the App Store's latest version. Stop cancels it and deletes the download. If that version is already staged, by Get latest, a drop or a dump, nothing is downloaded and the pane says "Already have <version>" (a copy from Get an older version doesn't count). The button then reads Get Again, which asks first, then downloads, decrypts and stages it again. If your Apple ID doesn't have the app yet and it's free, the button becomes Get (free). Graft asks first, then adds the app to your Apple ID's purchases at no cost, as Get in the App Store would, and downloads it. A paid app shows Open in App Store instead. Buy it there, then get it in Graft. Add App's Search offers "Get it from the App Store after adding" once the App Store is set up.

When a new version breaks a tweak, you can go back to one that worked. Get an older version…, beside Get latest on the app's pane, lists the versions the App Store still has for your Apple ID, newest first, with each one's date. Graft reads ten at a time, and Show More reads the next ten. Press Get on one, and Graft downloads, decrypts and stages it as Get latest does. Graft then holds the app at that version: its builds use it, and the pane says "Held at 1.2.0 · newest 1.4.0" instead of "update available". Get latest from App Store lets go of the hold and gets the newest version again. The hold is the app's preferred version, which Edit App also shows. A preferred version set in Edit App is a hold too; Get latest sets it back to latest. Only apps your Apple ID has. If it doesn't have the app yet, get it first. Apple doesn't serve every old version. One it won't describe or hand over says so, and you can pick another. The App Store sometimes has more than one build with the same version number. Graft numbers them from the oldest, so "1.2.0 (build 1 of 2)" is the older and "1.2.0 (build 2 of 2)" the newer, and hovering over one says which it is. Show More renumbers them when it finds an older one. Getting one of those builds holds the app at that build: the pane says "Held at 1.2.0 (build 1 of 2)", and builds use that build even when the other is staged too. A version typed in Edit App holds by number only: changing the preferred version there lets go of the build, and saving Edit App with it unchanged keeps it. In Terminal, graft --set-app-options --app <name> --preferred-version <version> holds that version by number. Dropping an IPA of the held version on the app, or decrypting it from a jailbroken device, holds the app at that version by number, with a warning: Graft can't tell which build an IPA it didn't download is, so builds use the one you gave it. If the connection stalls, the list stops, and Try Again picks up where it stopped. A version that stalls twice in a row is marked as unavailable, and the list goes on. Some apps refuse to run once they're too old, and ask you to update. A version that's already staged is held without downloading it again, unless another build shares its number: a staged copy could be either, so Graft downloads the build you picked. Graft counts only the builds it has read: one with the same number further down, past Show More, isn't counted yet, and the staged copy is held by number. Show More first if you think there's another. An old version may be one UnfairPlay can't verify (see Decrypts UnfairPlay can't verify). In Terminal, graft --appstore-versions --app example lists the versions with their ids, and graft --appstore-get --app example --version-id <id> gets one and holds the app at it; see App Store in the CLI Reference.

The downloaded IPA carries your Apple ID and your license for the app. Graft keeps it in a private temporary directory, deletes it afterward, and runs UnfairPlay with --strip-account-data. It doesn't rely on that flag. Every IPA Graft stages, from any source, has iTunesMetadata.plist (your Apple ID and account ids) and every SC_Info/ license directory removed, and is checked for them before it goes into the cache. An IPA staged by an earlier version is cleaned the first time a build uses it, and so is anything a re-install or a Mac install hands over. If the cache can't be written (a full or read-only disk), the build warns and goes on from a cleaned copy instead. Only when no clean copy can be made does it stop, rather than ship the data. A sideload archive keeps the license files its signature seals, since removing them would break the install. Rebuild it to get rid of them. What gets staged, built and put on a device doesn't identify you.

UnfairPlay checks the decrypted pages against Apple's own hashes. If it can't (some older apps), Graft refuses the IPA and offers Use it anyway…, which says what that risks, then runs the same get or drop again. If such an app crashes at launch, the decrypt is the likely cause.

Tweaks from Canister or an APT repository go into your tweaks library, and from there you attach them to an app. Find tweaks under Canister or in your Repos. Download them into Tweaks. Press Attach… on the app's pane. A .deb or .dylib you already have goes into the tweaks folder too.

Canister searches canister.me. A download by package id is checked against Canister's published SHA-256, when Canister has one, and comes from the repository the result names. Repos adds APT repositories and lists their packages. Free repositories only; repos that need a login or payment aren't supported. Tweaks lists your library (~/.config/graft/tweaks/), checks it for newer published versions when you ask, and updates a tweak, re-pointing the apps that use it. Deleting one an app still uses asks first, and offers Detach and Delete. Deleted tweaks go to the Trash. Graft names each download itself, <package id>_<version>.deb (with its architecture when the .deb names one). It keeps a download only if it's a .deb of the package and version it asked for, and never replaces a different tweak of the same name: delete that one first if you want the new one. Graft remembers where each tweak came from, and looks for its updates only there. For a tweak Graft has no record of, it finds where the file most likely came from, and asks you once: after you confirm one update, that source is on record. An update it can't verify (where the tweak came from isn't on record, the source doesn't use HTTPS, or it lists no checksum) says why on the tweak's row, and Update asks before it downloads it. Updating an app (Update & Install on its pane, or graft --update) also updates every tweak it uses that has a newer build from where it came from, once for all the apps that share it. While an update of an app runs, the Update button in Tweaks for the tweaks that app uses waits until it's done. See Updating your apps.

cyan bundles ElleKit as CydiaSubstrate and adds a few common frameworks when a tweak links them, but not every shared library a tweak may link against (color or settings libraries, for example). If a build fails with Library not loaded: @rpath/libexample.dylib, put a sandbox-compatible copy of that library in the tweaks folder and attach it to the app, as you would a .deb.
Tweaks built for RootHide depend on libroothide.dylib, which doesn't exist outside a jailbreak. Use the rootless build from the developer's own repository or releases.

Build & Install builds an app with its tweaks and pushes it into LiveContainer. With a paid account, Sideload delivery installs it as a normal app instead. Press Build & Install. LiveContainer delivery: Graft pushes the IPA into LiveContainer's Documents. Open LiveContainer on the device and import it from there. That's when LiveContainer signs it and the tweaks start loading. Sideload delivery (paid only): Graft signs the IPA with your certificate and installs it as a normal app. Build & Install waits until the app has a decrypted IPA and an iPhone or iPad is connected, and says which it's waiting for; Build for this Mac and Export IPA… wait for the IPA too. To build without installing, turn on Skip install in Build options. To sign on your iPhone or iPad instead, or install with TrollStore, Export IPA… in Build options saves the IPA unsigned. See Exporting an IPA. Builds lists every build, with its log and archive. See Building.

Each app has a delivery mode, LiveContainer or Sideload. An app added without one is LiveContainer with a free Apple ID and Sideload with a paid account. Add App starts on that one too, or on the one you chose last; a free Apple ID has only LiveContainer. Graft writes the mode whenever it adds an app, so an app keeps its mode if the config later changes account. Change it in the app's Edit sheet.

LiveContainer delivery builds the tweaked IPA unsigned and pushes it into LiveContainer's Documents folder over USB or Wi-Fi. You then import it inside LiveContainer, which runs it as a guest app. Why this is the main path: a guest app keeps its original bundle id, and some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id. It also needs no provisioning profile of its own, so zsign, the profile and the device-in-profile checks are skipped for these builds. How a delivery works: Build & Install pushes Documents/<name>.ipa into LiveContainer. The app's pane then names the device and reminds you to import it. On the device, open LiveContainer. The IPA is in its Documents; import it as an app. LiveContainer signs it on import, and that is when the tweaks start loading. Optionally remove the pushed IPAs afterward, with Clean up in the device's LiveContainer section. Delivering is not installing: Graft can see what it put in Documents, not whether you imported it. See Delivery state.

Sideload delivery signs the IPA with zsign, using your .p12 and profile, and installs it on the device as a normal top-level app. The device's UDID must be in the profile. Use this for apps that don't care about their bundle id or signing team. On a free Apple ID, building, re-installing or adding a sideload app is refused. On iOS 16 and later, an app signed with a development profile opens only with Developer Mode on. Graft checks before building one and stops if it's off. A real build first makes the switch appear in Settings › Privacy & Security › Developer Mode, which iOS hides until a development app is installed: turn it on there, and confirm after the device restarts. The device's page shows whether it's on. Ad hoc and enterprise profiles don't need it, nor do the apps you import into LiveContainer. A LiveContainer Graft installs does: it's signed with a development profile. Set Up LiveContainer… shows whether Developer Mode is on.

Build & Install runs this pipeline. Build options (beside it) picks the device and can build without installing. It can also export the IPA unsigned instead (see Exporting an IPA). Pre-flight. Tools, signing files, password, device, and that the device is in the profile. Only what the delivery mode needs is checked. Settings › Preflight, and graft --check in Terminal, check the same without building. There, no device connected is information ("not connected"), not a failure; a build that installs still needs one. Source IPA. The decrypted IPA staged in ~/.cache/graft/ipas/. Decryption check. The load commands of every Mach-O. Any that is still encrypted is reported as a warning naming the binary, and the build carries on. Inject. cyan, with the app's tweaks and options. The original bundle id is kept by default. cyan's output is meant to be re-signed: its modified binaries carry stale signatures until then. Every delivery re-signs before anything runs: zsign for Sideload, LiveContainer on import, SideStore or PlayCover on install. A LiveContainer build that isn't installed is for one of those signers. Sign (Sideload only). zsign with your .p12 and profile. Archive. Copy the result to ~/.cache/graft/built/. Deliver. Push into LiveContainer, or install on the device. Record. Write the build to ~/.local/state/graft/log.sqlite and apply archive retention. Stop ends the build where it is. A stopped build shows as Stopped, not as a failure, and adds no row to Builds.

section: Which device a build goes to
text: With nothing picked, a build goes to the default device when it's connected, else to the only other device connected. With several connected and none of them the default, the app pane's bar asks you to pick one, and Build & Install waits until you do. Change on the bar lists the connected devices, with their iOS version and, for a LiveContainer app, whether LiveContainer is on them. Picking one sends the next Build & Install there only ("Next Build & Install: iPad Air via LiveContainer · then back to iPhone 15 Pro"); the ✕ clears it, and it clears itself once that build starts installing or succeeds. A build that fails or is stopped before installing keeps it for the retry. A picked device that's unplugged stops Build & Install too, until you plug it in or clear the pick. Build options' Device picker sets the same pick. Updates don't use it: an update installs on every device the app is on. The menu also makes a device the default. In Terminal, --device <UDID> does the same for one build, and that device must be connected. When a build goes somewhere other than the default, its log says where and why. With no device connected, Build & Install waits, and the bar says to connect one. A device that's locked, or asking whether to trust this Mac, is connected but can't be read: the bar and the device's row in the sidebar say to unlock it and tap Trust, and Graft reads it again on its own, within a few seconds at first and every half minute after. For a LiveContainer app, a device without LiveContainer can't take the build: the bar says so and offers Set Up LiveContainer… for that device, over the app pane. With a paid account it also says you can switch the app to Sideload with Edit…. When a Sideload build signed with a profile Graft makes, or installing LiveContainer, goes to a device added to your developer account since you last saved App Store Connect in Settings, Graft reads the account's devices again first and saves the new list. A profile you made yourself isn't changed. Graft never registers a device.

Builds lists every build, with its saved log (View log…). A build's archive can be delivered again without rebuilding (Re-install…), or shown in Finder (Reveal in Finder). Re-install… asks first. It names the app, the build (its version and when it was made) and the iPhone or iPad it installs on: the one the build went to, else your default device, else the first one connected. When that device isn't connected, it says so and installs nothing. Return re-installs, and Escape cancels. A re-install goes out the way the archive was built: an unsigned LiveContainer archive is never installed as a top-level app, and a zsign-signed one is never pushed into LiveContainer. If the app's delivery mode has changed since, rebuild it. After each successful build, all but the newest archive_keep archives per app version go to the Trash (default 2; 0 keeps only the build just made). Grouping by version means rebuilds of one version never push out the last build of an older version, so you can always roll back to a version you shipped. Builds you can re-install are kept first. An archive left by a build whose install failed only keeps a slot none of those needs. Archives go to the Trash, not straight to deletion, so the space comes back when you empty it. Staged source IPAs are never pruned. Clean up old builds… in Builds does the same at your archive_keep: it says how many archives would go to the Trash, and moves them when you confirm. Useful after lowering the setting. The button is disabled while a build runs. A clean-up never moves an archive that is still in use. A build holds a lock from the moment it archives its IPA until its history entry is written, and a re-install holds it until the archive is delivered. A Mac install copies a built archive under the lock and hands PlayCover the copy, since PlayCover reads the file after Graft has returned. A clean-up you start waits up to 30 seconds for them to finish, then stops with an error and moves nothing. A build's own clean-up doesn't wait: if another build is delivering, it skips this time and says so, and the next build catches up. Two clean-ups at once take turns.

The app list and each app's pane say whether building now would produce something different from what was last delivered. On every delivery Graft records a SHA-256 over what determines the build: the source IPA's bundle id and version, each tweak's filename and contents, the cyan options and the delivery mode. Comparing that with what the config would produce now gives one of: State Means never Nothing has been delivered for this app. stale Something changed since the last delivery; the reasons say what (for example some-tweak.deb rebuilt since delivery or app version changed: 1.2.3 → 1.3.0). current Matches the last delivery. unknown Graft can't tell (for example a tweak file it can't read, or no staged IPA), and says so instead of guessing. Tweak contents are hashed, not just names, because a tweak rebuilt from source keeps its filename. The source IPA is identified, not hashed. Limits worth knowing: Delivered is not installed. For LiveContainer, Graft knows it wrote the file, not whether you imported it. Checking the device lists LiveContainer's Documents and can only downgrade a state: a missing file means the record is out of date, but a present file doesn't prove an import. Checking the device looks on the device the app was last delivered to, and says which ("Checked iPad mini — the record still stands"). It leaves sideload apps alone. A re-install of an archive that a recorded push shipped, byte for byte (usually the newest build), is compared like that push. Any other re-installed archive reads stale, because what went into it wasn't recorded. None of this blocks a build.

Graft checks your apps for updates at launch and once a day while it's open: a newer version on the App Store, a newer build of a tweak an app uses, or a build that changed since it was last installed. An app with something to update shows an arrow mark in the sidebar, and its pane says what: "Update available: App Store 1.2.0 · 1 tweak". Update & Install (or Update Tweaks & Install, or Install Update) shows what will change, app by app, and each device it installs on, then does it when you choose Update: the tweaks, the App Store download, one build, and an install on each device. Update All, above the apps when two or more apps have an update, does the same for each of them. An update installs on every device the app is on: each iPhone or iPad you've delivered it to, and only the ones that need it. It never adds a device, and the device picked for the next Build & Install doesn't apply. A device that isn't connected, even one unplugged during the update, waits: the app's pane says so ("iPad mini isn't connected: it'll update when it is"), and the app's other devices still update. When you connect it, Graft checks again within 10 minutes and offers its install. An update that only waits for a device doesn't mark the app in the sidebar or count in Update All. For a device you no longer use (sold, reset, or retired), Stop updating ("Stop updating Example on iPad mini"), in the menu beside its line on the pane or in the confirmation, stops updating that app there. It changes nothing on the device, and lasts until you install that app on that device again. Graft never buys or claims an app, and never moves an app off a version you're holding it at: that app still gets its tweak updates and install. After you re-install an older build on a device, or when the last install can't be found there, the pane says so and offers Install Update for that device (one for each, when there are several), for you to press. It's a Build & Install to that device; Graft doesn't install it on its own. When a tweak is shared, its other apps need an install too: the confirmation says which, and Also install … now adds them. A tweak updates only from where it came from: the repo or Canister repository you fetched it from. The confirmation says where each one comes from. When Graft can't verify an update (where the tweak came from isn't on record, that source doesn't use HTTPS, or it lists no checksum for it), the confirmation says why, and the tweak updates only if you turn on Trust this source. You're trusting the update the confirmation shows: if the source offers something else by the time it runs, Graft doesn't update that app and says so. On its own, such an update doesn't mark the app in the sidebar or count in Update All; the app's pane says "1 tweak to confirm". Stop stops at once, except during an install or while a tweak is being swapped in, which finish first. Stop Now cancels that install, and after three minutes Force Stop ends it outright. The progress shows each device's install under its app, and how it went. Try Again, for every app or for one device, picks up where it stopped. LiveContainer apps end up in LiveContainer's Documents on each device, to import there. Before the App Store is set up on this Mac (Settings › App Store), an update doesn't download from it: the pane says so, with Open Settings. On an Intel Mac, a newer App Store version shows, and can't be downloaded: drop a newer decrypted IPA on Source IPA instead. With Graft's Intel download on an Apple silicon Mac, Graft.zip can download it. A check that can't reach the App Store or canister.me, as when your Mac is offline, keeps what the last online check found while nothing has changed on this Mac. After a change (an IPA you staged, an install, a device you stopped updating), it shows what Graft knows without the network until it can check again. Graft tries again within the hour, and the confirmation says when it couldn't check online. Settings › Updates › Check my apps for updates turns the daily check off, and the checks after a get, build, tweak update, update, change to an app's options or tweaks, or device change. With it off, Graft checks only when you press Check for updates now, there, in the sidebar or on an app's pane, and the Update buttons show what that check found. Beside the button, it says how the check went: up to date, how many apps have updates, or that it couldn't check. The check sends your apps' bundle IDs to Apple's App Store lookup and your tweaks' package IDs to canister.me, and nothing that identifies you or your Mac. It opens no connection to your iPhone or iPad and reads nothing from the keychain. In Terminal, graft --update does the same; see Building in the CLI Reference.

On an Apple silicon Mac, an app's pane has Build for this Mac, which makes the build loadable under PlayCover and hands it to PlayCover. (On an Intel Mac, PlayCover can't run, and the button is disabled.) A staged IPA or an archived build can be handed over too. Some tweak libraries import iOS private frameworks that macOS doesn't have; for these Mac builds Graft bundles a minimal stand-in instead. iPhone and iPad builds are never changed this way. Graft.app carries that stand-in prebuilt, so a Mac build needs no Xcode. A graft installed with pipx builds it on demand and needs full Xcode for that; see The CLI without the app. Some tweaks need an iOS framework that macOS doesn't have at all. Graft won't build such a tweak for this Mac, or hand over a build that has one, and says which tweak, by its name in the Tweaks library, and which framework. iPhone and iPad builds can still use it. A framework the app itself links only gets a warning. After handing a build over, Graft waits up to two minutes for PlayCover to finish installing it, and says when it has. If it hasn't by then, check PlayCover's window; if the install failed there, Install to Mac… on the build's row in Builds tries again. Stop ends the wait, not the install. PlayCover has two settings per app that matter here: keymapping, which turns clicks into touches for games, and PlayChain. On an app's first handoff Graft turns both off and says so, because keymapping makes a non-game's clicks miss and PlayChain crashed apps the first time they saved a login. After that Graft keeps whatever you set in PlayCover: turn keymapping back on for a game, and it stays on when you rebuild. Not every iPhone or iPad app runs under PlayCover, even without tweaks: some open to a blank window, can't open their data, or have buttons that don't respond. If an app doesn't work, try it without tweaks first (Install to Mac… on its IPA in the Cache pane); if that fails too, PlayCover can't run that app. Graft doesn't include PlayCover, and doesn't download or install it. When PlayCover isn't installed, Build options says so above Build for this Mac, and Get PlayCover opens PlayCover's releases page on GitHub in your browser. You can still build first: once PlayCover is installed, Install to Mac… on the build's row in Builds hands it over. If a handover fails because PlayCover isn't installed, the error names the same page.

If you sign apps on your iPhone or iPad, with an on-device signer and a certificate service, or install them with TrollStore, Graft can give you the IPA instead of delivering it. Export IPA… in Build options builds the app as far as injecting its tweaks, then saves that IPA where you choose. What the file is. The app's decrypted IPA with its tweaks injected and the app's options applied, with your Apple ID's purchase data removed. It isn't signed: the binaries cyan changed need re-signing before iOS runs them. What to do with it. Put it on your iPhone or iPad (in Files, say) and open it in your on-device signer, which signs it with your certificate and installs it. Or install it with TrollStore. What Graft doesn't do. It signs nothing and sends nothing to a device, whatever the app's delivery mode, so a free Apple ID can export a Sideload app too. Graft only saves the file; moving it to the device is up to you. It isn't a build in Builds. An export adds no row to the build history and keeps no log, and archive clean-up never touches the file. For your own devices. It's an app your Apple ID owns or got for free. The Save panel asks before replacing a file that's already there. Graft builds the file in a temporary folder of its own and moves it to where you chose once it's done, so a stopped or failed export leaves nothing in your folder. Graft won't save into its own folders for staged IPAs and archived builds, which it cleans up itself. In Terminal, graft example --export-ipa ~/Desktop/Example.ipa does the same; see Building in the CLI Reference.

Graft pushes builds into the LiveContainer already on your device, and with a paid account it can install and update one itself. If LiveContainer is already on the device through SideStore, AltStore, iloader or Impactor, Graft uses it as it is. With a paid account Graft can also install and update LiveContainer itself, signed with your certificate so that guest apps keep their logins.

A device's pane has a LiveContainer section. It lists what is installed and who manages it, on either account. Set Up LiveContainer… does the whole setup in one sheet. With a paid account, its Set Up button checks the device against your developer account (reading the registered devices again if the device is new to them), installs LiveContainer from its own GitHub releases, and puts the certificate on the device. It stops at a step that fails and says what's left. After a failed certificate step, Set Up again puts the certificate on without installing again. Install / Update LiveContainer and Put certificate on device are in the sheet too, one step at a time. While a step runs, the sheet stays open until it ends or you press Stop. The sheet then lists the steps on the device, naming it: Import Certificate in LiveContainer's Settings, JIT-Less Diagnose, import your apps, and Convert to Shared App. LiveContainer asks for your .p12's password on the device; Graft can't type it for you. Selecting I imported the certificate takes the certificate off the device at once. Set Up and Install / Update LiveContainer need an App Store Connect key. Without one, the sheet says so, with Open Settings. They install one LiveContainer, the primary, unless more are on the device already; select 2 and 3 for side-by-side copies. The sheet also shows whether Developer Mode is on, which a LiveContainer from Graft needs on iOS 16 and later, with Check again for after the device restarts. With a free Apple ID, the sheet has no Set Up button. When LiveContainer is already on the device, it says which version it found, and the one step left is Import Certificate from SideStore. Otherwise it links to SideStore and iloader, which install LiveContainer with your Apple ID. Then it lists the same steps on the device. Where SideStore or AltStore is on the device, Set Up is disabled, and the sheet's first step is Import Certificate from SideStore. While a certificate Graft put on the device is still there, the section says so, with Remove it. Clean up is there whenever the device has a LiveContainer, whoever installed it.

Up to three LiveContainers can be installed side by side, as com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM> (the primary), com.kdt.LiveContainer2.<TEAM> and com.kdt.LiveContainer3.<TEAM>. Every installer names them this way, with its team id, so Graft finds them on the device by bundle id: a ten-character team id after the name, whatever team it is, in any letter case. A free Apple ID needs no team id in the config. System apps count too, so a LiveContainer that TrollStore or a jailbreak installed (often as plain com.kdt.livecontainer) is found, and so is one an on-device re-signer gave some other suffix.

section: Which one a build pushes into
text: In this order: the app's pin (the LiveContainer picker in its Edit sheet, or lc_bundle_id: in config.yaml), in any letter case, or the id without its team suffix when that names exactly one. A pin that names nothing installed, or an app that isn't LiveContainer, stops the build with what was found; it's never quietly ignored; the only LiveContainer on the device, whatever its bundle id; with a paid account, the configured team's primary; the only primary (com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM>, or plain com.kdt.livecontainer). Anything else stops the build with a list of what was found. That includes plain com.kdt.livecontainer next to a com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM>: Graft can't tell which one you import from, so it asks you to pin one rather than guess. A build finds out before it injects anything: the push's target, and whether its <app>.ipa name is free there, are checked ahead of cyan. The sidebar names the LiveContainer a push would use, found the same way.

Installing LiveContainer needs an App Store Connect API key (Settings › App Store Connect) to fetch profiles. It also needs the App IDs above (plus the primary's extensions) registered at developer.apple.com with the App Groups capability and the group group.com.SideStore.SideStore.<TEAM> assigned. App groups can't be assigned through the API; if one is missing, the error names the App ID. On a device where AltStore or SideStore manages LiveContainer, Graft won't install over it, because replacing those copies would break every guest app signed through them. Update through AltStore or SideStore instead.

Put certificate on device is for a LiveContainer Graft installed: it has no AltStore to take a certificate from, and its JIT-less mode needs one. Import it in LiveContainer's Settings, then select I imported the certificate in the sheet, or press Remove it on the device's pane. Until then the certificate sits where guest apps can read it.

Graft never deletes or replaces a file in LiveContainer's Documents unless it knows the file is its own: a delivery record for that device and that LiveContainer, or, with no record (after a state reset, say), the file's SHA-256 matching one of that app's archived builds. Clean up removes only the IPAs Graft's deliveries recorded and a certificate it recorded pushing, and retires those records, so a file you later put there under the same name is yours. An AppleDevelopment.p12 with no record (one you put there yourself) is reported and left in place. Putting the certificate on the device replaces it only when its bytes are your configured .p12. A build whose IPA name (<app>.ipa) is already taken by a file that isn't Graft's stops instead of overwriting it. Rename or remove that file in the Files app, then build again. A re-push of Graft's own earlier delivery replaces it as before.
Put the graft command on your Mac, either from Graft.app or with pipx. Graft in Terminal is optional; everything in the User Guide works without it.

In Graft.app, open Settings › Command-line tool and press Install graft for Terminal. It links the app's own graft into ~/.local/bin. If ~/.local/bin isn't on your shell's PATH, the section shows the line to add to your shell's startup file, with a Copy button. Open a new Terminal window afterward. The command runs the CLI inside the app, so it updates with the app, and Terminal and the app can't drift apart. If another graft is already in ~/.local/bin (a pipx install, say), the section says where it points and offers Replace it…. If a graft earlier on your PATH would win, it says that one is what Terminal runs. Move Graft.app to Applications first: the button won't link a copy running from a disk image or from where macOS put a downloaded app it moved aside.

To use Graft without the app, or to run it from source, install the CLI with pipx: pipx install git+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft # brew install pipx, if you need it pipx ensurepath pipx ensurepath adds ~/.local/bin to your PATH, so open a new terminal afterward for the graft command to be found. It needs Python 3.11 or later (the test suite passes on 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14). Graft.app never uses a pipx install. It always runs the copy inside it. To update it, run pipx reinstall graft-ipa. Once a new version is tagged on GitHub, pipx upgrade graft-ipa works too.

A pipx install doesn't include the tools Graft.app carries. Install the ones you use yourself: Tool Used for Install cyan (pyzule-rw) injecting tweaks pipx install --force https://github.com/asdfzxcvbn/pyzule-rw/archive/04a40f2aa65ec9cb36127f74d52ae4ef71377c50.zip (the commit tagged v1.4.4, the release Graft is tested with) zsign signing, for Sideload delivery (paid only) brew install zsign ipatool 2.8.0 App Store downloads graft --appstore-status prints the commands that download the release for your Mac's processor and put it at ~/.local/bin/ipatool. Use 2.8.0: 2.8.1 has a download bug, and Graft refuses it. UnfairPlay v0.4.0 decrypting App Store downloads, on Apple silicon A Go program, built from source to ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/unfairplay. graft --appstore-status prints the clone, checkout and go build commands. Full Xcode, selected (sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer) a PlayCover build whose tweak links an iOS private framework The stand-in framework is compiled with Xcode's iOS SDK, which the Command Line Tools don't have. Only such a build needs it, and only at that step; --check doesn't look for it. graft --check lists each missing tool with the command that installs it, and only the tools your apps' delivery modes use: zsign only when some app sideloads (or, on a paid config with no apps yet, since a new app sideloads by default). The brew commands need Homebrew, and --check says so when it isn't installed. Neither kind of install needs libimobiledevice or the Xcode Command Line Tools for iPhone and iPad builds: Graft reads binaries and installs apps itself, through pymobiledevice3.

cyan and zsign: Graft.app's own copy, then your PATH. config.yaml has no setting for either. ipatool and UnfairPlay: a path you set in config.yaml, then Graft.app's copy, then their usual install location, then your PATH (so a Homebrew ipatool is found too). Set them in an appstore: section (ipatool:, unfairplay:, unfairplay_models:), as full paths starting with / or ~/. A relative one is ignored, with a warning each time Graft runs, and read as not set. A path you set that points at nothing (you removed that ipatool, say): Graft.app, and the graft it links for Terminal, run their own copy instead, and --appstore-status notes the setting it passed over. Remove the key to stop the note. A pipx graft reports the tool as missing at that path. An appstore.ipatool of ~/.local/bin/ipatool, or an appstore.unfairplay of ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/unfairplay, counts as not set, so Graft.app's copy still comes first. --appstore-status says so for ipatool, and marks the UnfairPlay that runs "(bundled)". To make your own ipatool win, put it somewhere else and set the path. Without unfairplay_models:, Graft uses UnfairPlay's own default: UNFAIRPLAY_MODEL_DIR if set, else ~/Library/Application Support/unfairplay/models. Setting up decryption in Graft.app always uses Graft.app's own UnfairPlay, because that step runs it as root. --check and --appstore-status say which copy they found, and mark Graft.app's own "(bundled)".

Symptom Likely cause killed: 9 from zsign Quarantine attribute on a zsign you installed: xattr -cr "$(which zsign)". A PlayCover build stops saying it needs Xcode The tweak links an iOS private framework, and the pipx CLI builds its stand-in with Xcode's iOS SDK. Install and select full Xcode, or build from Graft.app, which carries the stand-in.
The commands for a first build from Terminal, once with a free Apple ID and once with a paid Apple Developer account.

Do the device steps under Set up your Apple account first. graft --init # answer no to the paid-membership question graft --check # tools, the device, and LiveContainer on it graft --appstore-search "example" # find it: name, developer, price, bundle id graft --add-app https://apps.apple.com/app/id123456789 # delivery: livecontainer graft --provide-ipa ~/Downloads/Example.ipa --app example graft --attach-tweak some-tweak.deb --app example graft example # build and push into LiveContainer

section: With a paid Apple Developer account
text: graft --init # answer yes: asks for the .p12 and profile, copies # them into ~/.config/graft/ and writes config.yaml graft --set-p12-password # store the .p12 password in the Keychain graft --check graft --add-app https://apps.apple.com/app/id123456789 --delivery livecontainer graft --list # shows the name it was added under, e.g. "example" graft --provide-ipa ~/Downloads/Example.ipa --app example graft --search "some tweak" graft --fetch com.example.sometweak # downloads into ~/.config/graft/tweaks/ graft --attach-tweak some-tweak.deb --app example graft example

section: If --init couldn't read the team id
text: If --init couldn't read the team id from the profile, it writes team_id: REPLACEME. Set the real one with graft --set-settings --signing-team-id <TEAM> before --set-p12-password: the Keychain entry is keyed by team id, so --set-p12-password refuses until it's set. Instead of the Keychain, you can export the variable named by signing.cert_password_env. When that variable is set and not empty, builds use it rather than the Keychain's password, so unset it once you store a new password in the Keychain.

graft --init --account free and graft --init --account paid --p12 <file> --profile <file> do what answering the questions does, and are what the app runs. The paid one reads the .p12 password from stdin (one line), or asks for it without echo in Terminal, and makes the same checks as the app. Neither touches a config that doesn't parse. On a paid config, --account paid refuses unless given --replace (the app's Replace certificate and profile…), and --account free switches it to a free Apple ID (the app's Switch to a free Apple ID…): it removes the signing: section and keeps the apps, repos and settings. On a free config, --account paid adds the paid account (Add a paid account…). --dry-run checks everything and writes nothing. The interactive --init copies the files it's given as they are, so an expired profile shows up in --check, and a certificate the profile doesn't list only when the device refuses the install. --config <path> works with any of these, for a config somewhere else. The app always uses the default one.
The graft commands, grouped by what they do. Almost every command takes --json (see Scripting), and every one takes --config <path>. graft --help lists every flag but --describe (see Scripting).

graft --list # apps: bundle id, pin, tweaks, delivery state, store (--json: account, mode) graft --appstore-search "example" # iPhone apps that match, from this Mac's region's store graft --appstore-search "example" --country GB --limit 10 graft --add-app https://apps.apple.com/app/id123456789 [--delivery livecontainer] graft --add-app-manual --name example --bundle-id com.example.app --display-name Example --store-country GB graft --remove-app example # cached IPAs and build history are kept --appstore-search needs no Apple ID. It asks the public iTunes Search API and sends only the search term and a country code. Its table ends with the --add-app-manual line for the store it searched: pass --store-country as it shows, so the app's update checks ask the same store. --country takes the two-letter code of a country with an App Store. A territory or UK is accepted as the store it uses (GB), with a note; a code with no store is refused. Without it, Graft uses the store of this Mac's region, or the US store if it can't read one or the region has none. --limit defaults to 25 and stops at 50. --json adds each result's icon, cached for a week in ~/.cache/graft/appstore-search-icons/.

graft --set-app-options --app example --delivery livecontainer # or sideload graft --set-app-options --app example --store-country GB # the store it's looked up in graft --set-app-options --app example --lc-bundle-id com.kdt.LiveContainer2.ABCDE12345 graft --set-app-options --app example --no-lc-bundle-id # drop the pin graft --set-app-options --app example --auto-profile # or --no-auto-profile --set-app-options also takes --preferred-version, --display-name, --[no-]keep-bundle-id, --[no-]strip-extensions, --[no-]strip-supported-devices and --compression-level. --auto-profile on a LiveContainer app still saves it, with a warning that it has no effect until the app is delivered by sideload.

graft --appstore-status # ipatool installed and signed in? UnfairPlay enrolled? graft --appstore-login # asks for the Apple ID, the password, then the code if Apple asks graft --appstore-logout graft --appstore-check # App Store version vs. your staged IPA, per app graft --appstore-get --app example # download, decrypt and stage the latest version (nothing if <bundle id>_<version>.ipa is staged) graft --appstore-versions --app example # the versions the App Store has for your Apple ID, newest first, with their ids graft --appstore-get --app example --version-id <id> # get that version, and hold the app at it graft --appstore-claim --app example # Get (free): only for an app the App Store lists at 0 --appstore-status prints the Terminal commands for whatever is missing, with the paths filled in. --appstore-login reads the Apple ID, the password and the code from stdin, and asks for each in a terminal (the password without echo). None of them is ever an argument. --allow-unverified with --appstore-get or --provide-ipa stages a decrypt UnfairPlay couldn't verify, with a warning. --again with --appstore-get downloads even when that version is already staged. A get downloads nothing when what it would get is staged already: for the latest, <bundle id>_<version>.ipa, as a get, --provide-ipa or --decrypt names it. A --version-id get stages <bundle id>_<version>_<version id>.ipa instead, which a plain get doesn't count, and counts the plain file only while no other build of that number has been listed. --appstore-versions reads the number and date of ten versions at a time, starting at --offset (--limit reads up to 50), and remembers them. The rest are listed by id. --version-id holds the app at the version it gets: preferred_version pins it, preferred_build names that build, and --appstore-check doesn't call a newer one an update. A plain --appstore-get lets go of the hold. See Get an older version. To set up decryption in Terminal, list the apps that can do it, save the script, run it as root, then finish as yourself: graft --appstore-enroll-candidates graft --appstore-enroll-command --app "/Applications/<that app>.app" > enroll.sh sudo /bin/sh enroll.sh graft --appstore-enroll-finish <the folder it prints> A graft that isn't Graft.app's own (a pipx install, or a Debug build), or an ad hoc signed Graft.app, has nothing to check root's UnfairPlay against, so --appstore-enroll-command refuses unless you pass --allow-unverified-helper.

graft --provide-ipa ~/Downloads/Example.ipa --app example graft --decrypt-check # what, if anything, is blocking a dump right now graft --decrypt com.example.app # dump an installed app by bundle id graft --decrypt-frontmost # dump whatever app is on screen graft --decrypt com.example.app --decrypt-backend bagbak graft --set-ssh-password # the device's root SSH password, into the Keychain graft --staged-ipas # every staged IPA, and anything stripped from it graft --cached-ipa example # which IPA a build of "example" would use graft --delete-staged com.example.app_1.2.3.ipa --decrypt-mode accepts only all, the default: bagbak's other modes dump bare binaries or extensions, which a build can't use. Pass --keep-encrypted-extensions to fail a dump instead of dropping extensions it couldn't decrypt.

graft --search "some tweak" # search canister.me graft --fetch com.example.sometweak # download a package by id (SHA-256 checked) graft --fetch com.example.sometweak --fetch-repository <repository_id> # from the repository a search listed (needed when several list it) graft --fetch https://example.com/some-tweak.deb --fetch-sha <sha256> graft --tweaks # list what is in tweaks_dir graft --attach-tweak some-tweak.deb --app example graft --detach-tweak some-tweak.deb --app example graft --delete-tweak some-tweak.deb # to the Trash; refused while an app uses it graft --tweak-updates # newer published versions? graft --update-tweak some-tweak.deb # download the newest and re-point the apps using it graft --update-tweak some-tweak.deb --trust-tweak <confirm_key> # one Graft can't verify, from --tweak-updates --json graft --add-repo https://repo.example.com graft --repos graft --repo-packages https://repo.example.com [--refresh] graft --remove-repo https://repo.example.com A --fetch by package id is checked against Canister's published hash, when Canister has one. A URL is checked only if you pass --fetch-sha. Either way Graft names the file (<package id>_<version>.deb), refuses one that isn't a .deb (or, by package id, isn't that package), refuses to replace a different tweak of that name, and records where it came from. A fetch by package id that more than one Canister repository lists names them and stops (exit 2): pick one with --fetch-repository. A tweak's updates come only from where it came from. --tweak-updates says whether each one is verified: that source is on record, uses HTTPS and lists a checksum for the new version. --update-tweak refuses one that isn't (exit 2), with why, unless you pass --trust-tweak with its confirm_key, which --tweak-updates --json gives. The key is for that update alone: if the source offers something else by then, it's refused too.

graft example # build and deliver graft example other # several apps in turn graft example --dry-run # show what would happen without doing it graft example --skip-install # build (and sign, for sideload) only graft example --device <UDID> # this build to that device (it must be connected) graft example --for-playcover # also make the build loadable on this Mac under PlayCover graft --install-to-mac <filename> # hand a staged IPA or an archived build to PlayCover graft example --export-ipa ~/Desktop/Example.ipa # inject the tweaks, save the IPA unsigned graft example -v # verbose, and keep the temp directory graft --update example # newer tweaks, newer App Store version, then build once and install on each device it's on graft --update --all --plan # what an update of every app would change; changes nothing graft --update example --with-affected # also install the apps that share an updated tweak graft --drop-update-target example --device <UDID> # stop updating it on a device that's gone --export-ipa signs nothing and touches no device (see Exporting an IPA). It takes one app, refuses --device, --skip-install and --for-playcover, and won't replace a file that's already there unless you add --overwrite. Under --json its last event before build-end is ipa-exported, with the file's path. Before it builds, it checks where the file goes, and that it can write a file in that folder. It writes the IPA to a hidden .<name>.<random>.partial file beside the path, then moves it into place, so a failed or stopped export leaves nothing behind. If graft is killed outright mid-write, that hidden file can be left there: it's safe to delete. The file's permissions are a new file's, as your umask sets them. How an export ends, by its exit status and, under --json, build-end's reason. The reason is null when the export worked, was stopped, or failed another way (cyan failing, say), which the exit status tells as it does for a build. Exit reason Meaning 0 null The IPA was written 2 exists A file is already at the path. --overwrite replaces it 2 bad-destination The path is a folder, its folder isn't there or is one of Graft's own, or it starts with ~name for a user this Mac doesn't have 1 unwritable graft can't write in that folder: its permissions, macOS's privacy controls, or a read-only disk 1 no-space The disk is full 1 write-failed Writing the file failed another way 4 no-ipa No IPA is staged for the app --skip-decrypt-check skips the decryption check. A Stop (SIGTERM) ends the build where it is: nothing is recorded as a failure, and under --json the last event is {"type": "build-end", "ok": false, "stopped": true, "error": null, ...}. --update updates the app's tweaks that have a newer build (each one once, for every app that uses it), gets the App Store's newer version (never buying or claiming one, and never for an app held at a version), then, one app at a time, builds once and installs on every device the app was installed on: the build's own install on the first (the default device first, then by name), and the same build on each of the others. It also installs a change staged since a device's last install, on that device. A device that isn't connected waits while the others install, a device that fails doesn't stop the others, and an app never installed is left to a build. A tweak update Graft can't verify is left out unless you confirm it with --trust-tweak <confirm_key>, the key --plan --json gives it (once per tweak); if that update changed since, the app isn't updated, and says so. --plan says what it would do, device by device, and changes nothing; it reads no keychain. Run it again to pick up where a failed or stopped update left off: it installs only where the app isn't up to date. A Stop during an install, or while a tweak is being swapped in, lets that finish first, and the devices after it aren't started; a second Stop ends the install too. See Updating your apps. --drop-update-target APP --device UDID stops updating an app on a device it was installed on, for a device that's gone (sold, retired or reset), until the app is installed there again. It changes nothing on any device.

graft --builds [--builds-app example] [--builds-limit 20] graft --build-log 42 # the saved log of build 42 (builds run with --json, as the app does) graft --reveal-build 42 # show its archived IPA in Finder graft --reinstall-build 42 # deliver that archive again, without rebuilding (same delivery mode only) graft --prune-builds --dry-run # what retention would remove graft --prune-builds [--keep 1] # apply it now graft --delivery-state [--app example] # would building now produce something different? graft --reconcile [--app example] # check the device first, then report --dry-run previews only a build, --export-ipa, --prune-builds, --init --account and --remove-data --items. Every other command refuses it, before doing anything, rather than running for real under a flag that said it wouldn't.

graft --lc-status # LiveContainers on each device, who manages them, upstream version graft --lc-install # paid only: install or update all three (default device, or --device) graft --lc-install --instances 1 # only the primary (comma list: 1,2,3) graft --lc-install --channel stable # stable instead of nightly (nightly is what upstream recommends) graft --lc-install --force # replace LiveContainers AltStore or SideStore manages graft --lc-push-cert # paid only: put your .p12 in the primary's Documents graft --lc-clean --cert-only # remove the certificate once imported graft --lc-clean # remove the certificate and the IPAs Graft pushed, wherever each went --lc-status and --lc-clean work with either account. --devices names the LiveContainer a push would use.
graft --devices # connected devices over USB and Wi-Fi graft --device-info [--device <UDID>] # storage, battery, Developer Mode graft --device-apps [--with-icons] # user apps on the device

graft --settings # the global settings graft --set-settings --default-device <UDID> # '' to unset graft --set-settings --archive-keep 3 graft --set-settings --signing-cert <file> --signing-profile <file> --signing-team-id ABCDE12345 graft --set-p12-password graft --set-portal --asc-key-id ABCDE12345 \ --asc-issuer-id 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 \ --asc-key-file ~/Downloads/AuthKey_ABCDE12345.p8 graft --setup-portal # the same key, with questions graft --clear-portal # remove it (the .p8 stays) graft --check-update # is a newer Graft out? (asks GitHub; downloads nothing) graft --download-update # download it into Graft's cache and check it (installs nothing) graft --remove-data # what Graft keeps outside Graft.app, with sizes graft --remove-data --items all # remove it (see Removing Graft); add --dry-run to preview Graft.app installs a download it checked with --install-update, which it runs as it quits; see Updating Graft. Removing Graft lists every item --items takes. --set-settings --signing-* refuses on a free config rather than write part of a signing: section, which would leave a config that no longer loads. To switch account in Terminal, run graft --init again: on a free config it offers to add a paid account, and on a paid one to switch to a free Apple ID, keeping apps, repos and settings either way.
A script drives graft with --json, as the Mac app does. The environment variables graft reads include the ones for running behind a proxy.

--json turns a command's output into newline-delimited JSON events on stdout. Every stdout line is one JSON object, and any command's narration and warnings go to stderr. This is how the Mac app talks to the CLI. Notices from before the command runs (a directory moved to its new name, an old environment variable still set) are log events with "source": "startup". --list starts with one account event, {"type":"account","account":"free"} or "paid", even when no apps are configured. The app events after it and the preflight-end event from --check carry the same account field. graft --describe prints the contract the app relies on: every flag and every event type. --help doesn't list it. A few commands don't answer in events. --init without --account refuses --json. --version, --setup-portal and the password prompts ignore it, and so do three whose output is fixed already: --build-log prints the saved log as it is (JSON Lines, since only builds run with --json save one), --describe always prints JSON, and --reveal-build prints nothing.

Variable Meaning the one named by signing.cert_password_env .p12 password: when set and not empty, used instead of the Keychain's GRAFT_SSH_USER, GRAFT_SSH_PASS, GRAFT_SSH_KEY SSH to a jailbroken device, for a dump GRAFT_FRIDA_IOS_DUMP where frida-ios-dump is cloned UNFAIRPLAY_MODEL_DIR UnfairPlay's own: where its model lives XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME move Graft's directories HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY (and the lower-case forms) send Graft's requests through a proxy REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_DIR trust another CA, such as a TLS-inspecting proxy's root Graft.app reads these from your login shell when it starts, and again when you press Check again (on the setup screen or beside Settings' PATH line) or Re-run in Preflight, at most once every 10 seconds. It runs the shell as an interactive login shell, given 5 seconds. csh and tcsh run as interactive shells, which read ~/.tcshrc or ~/.cshrc but not ~/.login. So a variable exported in ~/.zshrc or ~/.zprofile reaches the CLI it runs, as do your PATH additions and XDG_* directories. PYTHON* variables and the color switches (FORCE_COLOR, TTY_COMPATIBLE, TTY_INTERACTIVE, PY_COLORS, CLICOLOR_FORCE) are never passed on. If the shell doesn't answer, the app carries on without them (or, on a later Check again, with what it read before), and a startup file that hangs is stopped along with everything it started. On a Mac without the Xcode Command Line Tools, a startup file that runs one of their commands (git, say) can make macOS offer to install them when Graft starts, as opening a Terminal window would. Graft doesn't need them: cancel, or install them.

Graft's own requests (iTunes lookups, Canister, repos, LiveContainer's releases) honor the proxy variables. Graft.app's bundled Python trusts the CA certificates it ships (certifi) and /etc/ssl/cert.pem, never the macOS Keychain, so a proxy that re-signs TLS needs its root named in a CA variable: export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/corp-ca.pem (a PEM file holding the proxy's root, plus the public roots if you want the rest of the internet too). In Graft.app, and in the graft it links into ~/.local/bin, each of REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE and CURL_CA_BUNDLE is used only when it names an existing, readable file by an absolute path, and SSL_CERT_DIR only when it names an existing folder. Otherwise it's ignored, so a stale export can't break every connection. OPENSSL_CONF and OPENSSL_ENGINES are always ignored there: they're meant for another OpenSSL. The pipx CLI passes all of these through untouched. ipatool and UnfairPlay are Go programs and use the macOS trust settings, Keychain included.

Graft is fully scriptable: every action in the app is a graft command, and almost every command can answer in JSON. So an AI coding agent that runs Terminal commands on your Mac, such as Claude Code, can drive Graft for you from a request in plain English.

An agent can take the same steps you would, in order: search the App Store and add an app; get the app's IPA from the App Store, the latest version or an older one, or stage an IPA you give it; search Canister or your repos for tweaks, download them and attach them; build the app and deliver it to your iPhone or iPad, or export its IPA unsigned, for an on-device signer; update your apps: a newer App Store version and newer tweaks, then the build and the install; check what's out of date, what was last delivered, and why a build failed. It reads Graft's results and its hints as it goes, so it can tell you what went wrong and what to do next. graft --describe gives it the full list of commands, flags and events.

Set up Graft.app first: its first run, and for App Store downloads, Sign in and Set up decryption. In Graft.app, open Settings › Command-line tool and press Install graft for Terminal (see Installing the CLI). In a new Terminal window, graft --version prints Graft's version. Make a folder for the agent to work in, and save AGENTS.md from Graft's repository into it. It tells an agent how to call graft, how to read its answers, and what to leave to you. Some agents read a file with that name by themselves; with others, start by asking the agent to read it. Open your agent in that folder. The agent runs graft as you, with your config, apps and settings, just as if you typed the commands yourself.

"Add Example App from the App Store, attach the tweak com.example.sometweak from Canister, and install it to my iPhone through LiveContainer." "Search Canister for tweaks for Example App, show me what you find, and attach the one I pick." "Check whether any of my apps has a newer version on the App Store, or any of my tweaks a newer release, tell me what you'd update, and update the ones I pick." "My last build of Example App failed. Find out why and tell me what to do." "The new version of Example App broke my tweak. Get the version before it from the App Store, and rebuild it once I say yes."

section: What it does, and what it leaves to you
text: AGENTS.md lets an agent search, list and check things, add an app, download an app your Apple ID already has, fetch and attach tweaks, and preview a build with --dry-run, without asking. It exports an IPA only when you ask, saves it only where you say, and never sends the file anywhere. It asks before it replaces a file that's already there. It tells the agent to ask you first before: anything that changes your iPhone or iPad: a build that delivers to it, an update, installing or cleaning up LiveContainer, or a re-install; getting a free app your Apple ID doesn't have yet. Graft never buys anything: the agent asks before it adds a free app to your Apple ID's purchases, and a paid app is yours to buy in the App Store; getting the latest version of an app that's held at an older one, or at a preferred version you set in Edit App: that lets go of the hold (see Get an older version); updating a tweak from a source Graft can't verify (it doesn't know where the tweak came from, the source doesn't use HTTPS, or it lists no checksum); removing anything: an app, a tweak, a staged IPA or old builds. And it tells the agent never to: sign in to the App Store for you, or ask for your Apple ID password or the code Apple sends. You sign in in Graft.app; set up decryption, which needs your administrator password in macOS's own dialog. You press Set Up Decryption… yourself; ask for or type any other password: your Mac's, your .p12's or your device's SSH password; answer a keychain or password dialog for you. If one appears while the agent works, it says which command caused it. install a Graft update, or remove Graft's data, unless you ask for that yourself. Graft.app updates itself. Before an update (graft --update), the agent tells you what will change for each app and each device it installs on: every device that app was installed on, and no other. A device that isn't connected waits. The agent asks before --drop-update-target, which stops updating an app on a device that's gone. An update never buys or claims an app, and never lets go of a hold. An agent can still get things wrong. Read what it's about to do to your device before you say yes. LiveContainer delivery puts the IPA in LiveContainer's Documents on your device. Opening LiveContainer and importing it is still your step, as it is when you build from the app. On iOS 16 and later, a Sideload build signed with a development profile stops when Developer Mode is off on the device. Turning it on is yours to do, on the device (see Sideload). Graft is for personal use, whoever runs it: your own Apple ID, apps you own or get for free, on your own devices. Don't redistribute decrypted or modified IPAs.

The agent runs on your Mac and sees what Graft prints: your apps and tweaks, your devices' names and UDIDs, file paths in your home folder, and, from graft --appstore-status, the email of the Apple ID you signed in with. Your passwords stay in your login keychain and aren't part of that output. If the agent's AI model runs online, what the agent reads is sent to that service, and that service's terms apply to it. See Scripting & Environment for --json, and the CLI Reference for every command.

Graft stores its settings and each app's options in config.yaml, and its other files in folders of its own. Settings holds what most people change: the default device, how many archives to keep, the signing files on a paid account, the App Store Connect key, the App Store sign-in, and the paths Graft uses.
