Change on an app's bar picks another device for the next Build & Install only (see Which device a build goes to). Each app's Edit sheet holds its options. Everything is stored in ~/.config/graft/config.yaml ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/graft if set), which you can also edit by hand. A configured app looks like this: signing: # paid only; leave it out for a free Apple ID cert: ~/.config/graft/AppleDevelopment.p12 cert_password_env: GRAFT_P12_PASS # when set, used instead of the Keychain's profile: ~/.config/graft/wildcard.mobileprovision team_id: ABCDE12345 cache_dir: ~/.cache/graft/ipas tweaks_dir: ~/.config/graft/tweaks archive_keep: 2 # archived builds kept per app version # default_device_udid: <UDID> apps: example: bundle_id: com.example.app preferred_version: latest delivery: livecontainer # or sideload store_country: "GB" # the App Store it's looked up in # lc_bundle_id: com.kdt.LiveContainer2.ABCDE12345 # pin a LiveContainer tweaks: - some-tweak.deb # files in tweaks_dir cyan: display_name: Example keep_bundle_id: true # some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id strip_extensions: false strip_supported_devices: true compression_level: 6 The app re-reads your config each time its window comes back to the front, so a change made in an editor or in Terminal shows without a relaunch. If config.yaml doesn't parse, Settings says so at the top, shows the default paths and saves nothing until it's fixed. Fix it in an editor, and the notice clears when you come back to the window. Free or paid. A config with no signing: section (or an empty one) is a free Apple ID. signing: keys that end up at the top level (lost indentation) are an error naming them, not a free config. Add a paid account… asks only for the .p12 and the profile, then adds a signing: section to the config and keeps its apps, repos and settings. With a paid account an app with no delivery mode is a sideload app, so Graft writes LiveContainer delivery into each such app and says which. Nothing moves until you change one. Switch to a free Apple ID… removes the signing: section and keeps everything else. Apps with no delivery mode then go into LiveContainer. One set to Sideload stays set, and won't build until you switch it to LiveContainer. Replace certificate and profile… swaps in a new pair, its Keychain password and the signing: section, keeps everything else, and puts the old ones back if any step fails. When the new pair belongs to another team, the old team's Keychain password is removed. The paid setup checks that the .p12 opens with its password and that the profile lists its certificate and hasn't expired. It copies both files into the config folder (0600, never through a link). Bundle id. Some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id; keep_bundle_id: true (the default) preserves it. With keep_bundle_id: false cyan renames it (to new_bundle_id, or the original plus .plus) in both delivery modes, LiveContainer included. Renaming the bundle id also removes any Apple Watch app, which can't install under a new id. Per-app profiles (paid only). "Create the provisioning profile automatically" in an app's Edit sheet (auto_profile: true) has Graft create and cache a profile for the app through the App Store Connect API; profile: <path> points one app at a specific profile. Both apply to sideload builds only, and the option is locked on a LiveContainer app, which uses no profile. Make an API key at App Store Connect, then give it to Graft in Settings › App Store Connect. Graft checks the key by listing your devices, and only then copies the .p8 beside config.yaml. Setting a key replaces only the key and its devices. A profile_cache_dir you set by hand stays, and device_udids is refreshed every time with every enabled iPhone, iPad and iPod touch App Store Connect lists. To keep a list you curated, add device_udids_pinned: true to the app_store_connect: section. The lock file. Graft takes a lock on config.yaml.lock beside the config while it edits it, so the app and the CLI never write over each other. If you keep the config in a dotfiles repository and symlink it, add config.yaml.lock to that repository's .gitignore.

~/.config/graft/ ├── config.yaml ├── config.yaml.lock ├── AppleDevelopment.p12 ├── wildcard.mobileprovision ├── AuthKey_<KEY_ID>.p8 # App Store Connect API key ├── profiles/ # profiles made through that API └── tweaks/ # .deb and .dylib files ~/.cache/graft/ ├── ipas/ # staged decrypted IPAs (never pruned) ├── built/ # archived builds (newest archive_keep per app version) ├── artwork/ # cached app icons └── updates/ # a newer Graft, downloaded and checked, until it's installed ~/.local/state/graft/ ├── log.sqlite # build history and delivery records ├── build-logs/ # saved event log of each --json build (so every build from the app) ├── repos/ # cached APT repository indexes └── tweak-rollback/ # previous versions kept when a tweak is updated ~/.local/share/graft/ # tools you install for Graft (frida-ios-dump; UnfairPlay, for a pipx install) These four graft directories are owner-only (0700): Graft creates them that way and tightens them on every run if they aren't. Staged IPAs, archived builds, build logs and the .p12 and profile the setup copies are written 0600. Graft changes nothing outside these directories, and leaves alone a graft that is a symlink you made. The one exception is updating itself: it replaces its own Graft.app, moves the old one to the Trash, and writes what it did to ~/Library/Logs/Graft/update.log. Outside them, the App Store tools keep their own files: ipatool's sign-in in your login keychain, its session cookies in ~/.ipatool and its downloads in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool, and UnfairPlay's model in ~/Library/Application Support/unfairplay/models. Removing Graft lists everything.

When Graft goes online and what it downloads, including the one-time downloads on the first App Store action. Graft has no telemetry, analytics or crash reporting. Graft.app makes no connections of its own: its CLI does, for something you asked for or a pane you opened; to look up the icon of an app that has none yet; once a day to ask GitHub whether a newer Graft is out, and to download it; and once a day to check whether your apps and tweaks have updates. Settings › Updates turns off the daily checks and the download. Device names and UDIDs never leave your Mac. No Apple ID. A newer Graft is out, unless Settings › Updates turns automatic updates off (then when you choose Update) GitHub's release files (github.com), with nothing that identifies you or your Mac The new Graft.zip (Graft-Intel.zip for the Intel build), about 150 MB, once A paid account with an App Store Connect key makes a profile, or a build signed with a profile Graft makes, or a LiveContainer install, targets a device missing from the saved list (Graft lists your registered devices; it never registers one) Apple's App Store Connect API Provisioning profiles You sign in, get an app or an older version of one, list an app's older versions, or get a free one Apple's App Store, through the bundled ipatool Your sign-in, the license, the IPA, the versions' numbers and dates The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) PyPI (files.pythonhosted.org), and Apple's software CDN ipatool's Unicorn emulator (a few MB) and its App Store components (about 320 MB), once About that first App Store action: Graft.app doesn't include Unicorn. The bundled ipatool downloads Unicorn 2.1.4 from PyPI on first use, as upstream ipatool does, and checks it against the SHA-256 its source pins. Both downloads are cached in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool, so they happen once, and again only for a new version. Offline, that first App Store action stops with "ipatool needs to download its App Store emulator (Unicorn, from PyPI) the first time; connect to the internet and try again." UnfairPlay has no network code, and talking to your iPhone or iPad stays on your Mac and your local network. What Graft connects to lists every host, when, and what is sent.

Every host that Graft.app, the graft CLI, or a tool bundled in the app contacts: why, when, and what it sends. It was gathered by reading the code (graft_ipa/, Graft/Graft/, the bundled Python packages), the pinned sources of ipatool 2.8.0 and UnfairPlay 0.4.0, and the bundled binaries' strings. It covers Graft 2.0.2. Short version: Graft has no telemetry, analytics or crash reporting. It checks for updates: once a day while the app is open, the CLI asks GitHub for Graft's latest release, sending nothing that identifies you or your Mac (api.github.com, below). When there's a newer one, the CLI downloads its zip of your build (Graft.zip, or Graft-Intel.zip for the Intel build) from GitHub (github.com, below), checks it, and installs it when you quit Graft. Settings › Updates turns either off. It checks your apps for updates: at launch and once a day while the app is open, after a get, a build, a tweak update or an update, and when a device connects or disconnects while an update waits for one (at most every 10 minutes), the CLI looks up your apps' bundle ids in Apple's public App Store lookup (one request per App Store country) and your attached tweaks' package ids at canister.me, only for tweaks that didn't come from one of your repos, with no Apple ID and nothing that identifies your Mac (below). The check opens no connection to your iPhone or iPad and reads nothing from the keychain. Settings › Updates › Check my apps for updates turns all of these off; Check for updates now still checks, whether it's on or off. The app makes no connections of its own. Everything goes through the CLI and the tools it runs. Your Apple ID, your password and the 2FA code, if Apple asks for one, go only to Apple, through the bundled ipatool. You type them into Graft's sign-in sheet (Settings › App Store › Sign In…), or graft --appstore-login asks for them in Terminal. Graft passes them over stdin to ipatool's own prompts and never stores them. ipatool keeps the sign-in, including the password, in your login keychain. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's Unicorn emulator from PyPI and about 320 MB of App Store components from Apple, once. On an Intel Mac, and in the Intel build (Graft-Intel.zip) anywhere, Graft makes no App Store sign-in or download at all, so none of the ipatool hosts below is contacted. Searching the App Store and adding an app by name use Apple's public lookup and need no sign-in. Device UDIDs never leave your Mac.

The CLI sends User-Agent: graft/<version> (+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft) with every request it makes through requests. There are two exceptions. Downloading icon images (--artwork, and the icons of --appstore-search results) sends the library's default User-Agent. The update check and the update download send User-Agent: Graft, without the version. Bold marks user data. Host Contacted by When What's sent itunes.apple.com (/lookup) CLI: --add-app, --appstore-check, --update (and --update --plan), --artwork, the free-price check before --appstore-claim, and the version check before --appstore-get --add-app: when you add an app. The app also runs the other two on its own: --appstore-check when an app's detail pane opens; --artwork at launch, when the app list changes, and after a build or App Store get, but only for apps with no icon cached or in a cached IPA. The price check: when a get is refused for want of a license, and before Get (free). The version check: before Get latest from App Store, only when the app has an IPA staged (not with --again, or Get Again). --update asks once per store country, naming every app of that store in one request (bundleId=a,b,c). The App Store id from the URL you gave, or the app's bundle id, and the two-letter store the app came from (the one Search asked, or the one its URL names; else this Mac's region's store, then the US store if that one doesn't sell it). No account. itunes.apple.com (/search) CLI: --appstore-search When you type in Add App › Search: once you pause for half a second, for 2 or more characters, and only for a term not already searched in that sheet. Graft downloads and checks a newer version by itself, and installs it when you restart or quit.

Once a day while it's open (or when you choose Help › Check for Updates…), Graft asks GitHub whether a newer version is out. If one is, it downloads it in the background, then shows Restart to Update in a banner at the bottom of the main window. If you don't restart, it installs the update when you quit Graft. Each download updates from its own zip: Graft.zip for Apple silicon, Graft-Intel.zip for the Intel build. A release without yours has no update for your Mac yet, and Graft never installs the other one. A release that needs a newer macOS than your Mac has is no update for your Mac either: Graft downloads it once, finds it needs a newer macOS, deletes it and stays on the version you have. It doesn't download that release again until your Mac has that macOS. Before it calls a download ready, Graft checks it: the SHA-256 GitHub lists for it, then that the app inside is Graft, newer than yours, the same build as yours, signed with the same developer's Developer ID as yours and notarized by Apple. A download that fails any check is deleted, and the banner links to the release page instead. A Graft you built yourself, which has no Developer ID, doesn't update itself. The old Graft.app goes to the Trash, so you can put it back. Graft never installs while it's working (a build, an install, an App Store download and so on). It waits until that's done, or until you quit. Your config, apps and builds carry over, and so does your App Store sign-in. The Terminal command points into the app, so it updates too. The check and the download send nothing that identifies you or your Mac. What Graft connects to shows what they send.

Settings › Updates has three switches, all on to start with: Check for updates automatically is the daily check. With it off, Help › Check for Updates… still asks when you choose it. Download and install updates automatically is the background download. With it off, the banner offers Update, which downloads, checks and restarts when you choose it. Check my apps for updates is the daily check of your apps and their tweaks, not of Graft. Its line says what it sends: "Once a day, and after each get, build, tweak update, update or change to an app's options or tweaks, and when a device connects or disconnects while an update waits for one (at most every 10 minutes). Sends your apps' bundle IDs to Apple's App Store lookup and your tweaks' package IDs to canister.me. No Apple ID or Mac identifier." With it off, Graft checks only when you press Check for updates now, below it. See Updating your apps.

Graft can't update itself when it runs straight from Downloads (macOS runs a read-only copy of an app it hasn't moved), or from a folder your account can't change. The banner then says so and links to GitHub Releases: download the new Graft.zip (or Graft-Intel.zip) there and replace the Graft.app in /Applications. If an update can't be installed, Graft keeps the version you have, says so the next time it opens, and writes what happened to ~/Library/Logs/Graft/update.log.

graft --check-update asks GitHub whether a newer Graft is out, and downloads nothing. graft --download-update downloads it into Graft's cache and checks it, and installs nothing. With --json, --check-update prints one update-check event. If a download has found that the latest release needs a newer macOS than your Mac has, its update_available is false and needs_macos names that macOS ("15.0"); otherwise needs_macos is null.

Help › What's New… shows what changed in the latest release. It also opens by itself once, the first time a new version of Graft starts, on what's new since the version you used before. Show earlier releases adds the rest. The Changelog has every release.
What changed in each release of Graft, newest first. Each release's download is on GitHub Releases.

A tweak updates only from where it came from: the repo or Canister repository you fetched it from. Another repo that publishes the same package can't replace it in your apps. When Graft can't verify a tweak update (Graft has no record of where the tweak came from, the source doesn't use HTTPS, or it lists no checksum), the update confirmation says why and where the update comes from, and the tweak updates only if you turn on Trust this source. You're trusting the update the confirmation shows: if the source offers something else by the time it runs, Graft doesn't update that app, and says so. The Tweaks pane asks first too. Graft names each tweak it downloads (<package id>_<version>.deb, with its architecture when the package names one), keeps a download only if it's a .deb of the package it asked for, and never replaces a different tweak. Fetching from a Canister search takes the build from the repository the result shows. In Terminal, a fetch by package id that several Canister repositories list names them and asks you to pick one. A Canister repository recorded as a tweak's source whose address has moved counts as unverified. A copy of the LiveContainer certificate left in the temporary folder by a push that was killed is removed the next time Graft runs.

Updates for your apps. Graft now says when an app has something to update: a newer version on the App Store, a newer build of a tweak it uses, or a build that changed since it was last installed. The app shows an arrow mark in the sidebar, and its pane says what ("Update available: App Store 1.2.0 · 1 tweak"). Update & Install shows what will change and where it installs, then updates the tweaks, gets the App Store version, builds and installs, showing its progress as it goes. Update All, when two or more apps have an update, does the same for each of them. An update installs on every device the app is on: one build, then the same build on each. The confirmation lists each device, and the progress shows each install with its own result and Try Again. A device that isn't connected waits ("iPad mini isn't connected: it'll update when it is") while the others install, and its install is offered again once it's connected. A device that can't take the build, with Developer Mode off say, doesn't stop the others. An update that only waits for a device doesn't mark the app in the sidebar, and Stop updating ("Stop updating Example on iPad mini") stops waiting for a device you no longer use. Graft never buys or claims an app, and never moves an app off a version you're holding it at. When an updated tweak is shared, the confirmation names the other apps that use it, and Also install … now installs them too. After you re-install an older build on a device, the pane offers Install Update for that device instead of installing on its own. Stop during an update stops at once, except during an install or while a tweak is being swapped in, which finish first. Stop Now cancels that install, and after three minutes Force Stop ends it. Try Again picks up where it stopped. Quitting during an install waits for it to finish. A daily check of your apps. At launch, once a day while it's open, and after a get, build, tweak update or update, Graft checks your apps and their tweaks for updates. It sends your apps' bundle IDs to Apple's App Store lookup and your tweaks' package IDs to canister.me, and nothing that identifies you or your Mac. Settings › Updates › Check my apps for updates turns these checks off, and Check for updates now still checks when you want. Pick the device for a build. The app's bar says where the next Build & Install goes, and why. Change sends the next Build & Install to another connected device, then goes back to the default; a build that fails or is stopped before installing keeps the pick for the retry. With the default device unplugged, a build goes to the only other device connected, and with several connected, the bar asks you to pick one. Settings names a default device that isn't connected. A build signed with a profile Graft makes, or a LiveContainer install, to a device added to your developer account since you saved App Store Connect, reads the account's devices again first, so the profile includes it. A device that isn't registered is named in the error; Graft never registers one. Set Up LiveContainer. A device's pane sets up LiveContainer in one sheet. With a paid account, Set Up checks the device against your developer account, installs LiveContainer and puts the certificate on the device. The sheet then lists the steps to do on the device: importing the certificate, JIT-Less Diagnose, importing your apps, and Convert to Shared App. LiveContainer asks for your .p12's password on the device; Graft can't type it for you. With a free Apple ID, it links to SideStore and iloader instead. While a certificate Graft put on the device is still there, the device's pane says so, with Remove it. For a LiveContainer app, the bar offers Set Up LiveContainer… when the device it's building for has none. Developer Mode. On iOS 16 and later, an app signed with a development profile opens only with Developer Mode on. Graft now checks before it builds one. If it's off, the build stops, after making the switch appear on the device in Settings › Privacy & Security › Developer Mode, which iOS hides until then. The device's page shows whether it's on. In Terminal, --device-info reports developer_mode, and --list reports needs_developer_mode. Holds by build. When the App Store has two builds of one version, getting one holds the app at that build: the pane says "Held at 1.2.0 (build 1 of 2)", and builds use that build even when the other is staged too. Moving between those builds marks the app out of date, and the Cache pane marks the file the build uses. Dropping an IPA of the held version, or decrypting it from a jailbroken device, holds the app at that version by number, with a warning. Updates in Terminal. graft --update <app>, or --all, updates the app's tweaks, gets the App Store's newer version, then builds once and installs on every device the app was installed on. --plan says what it would do, device by device, and changes nothing. It never buys or claims an app or lets go of a hold, and installs only what changed: after you re-install an older build, it leaves that install to you. Run it again to pick up where a failed or stopped update left off; it installs only where the app isn't up to date. A Stop during an install lets the install finish, and a second Stop ends it. graft --drop-update-target <app> --device <UDID> stops updating an app on a device that's gone. AGENTS.md tells an AI agent how to use it. PlayCover keeps your settings. Graft turns off PlayCover's keymapping and PlayChain only on an app's first handoff, and says so. After that it keeps what you set in PlayCover: turn keymapping on for a game and it stays on when you rebuild. If PlayCover changes either one anyway, Graft puts yours back. Graft waits for PlayCover's install. After handing a build over, Graft waits up to two minutes and says "PlayCover installed Example 1.2.0". Build for this Mac, and Install to Mac… in Builds and the Cache, show "Waiting for PlayCover to install Example…" with Stop, which ends the wait, not the install. A tweak that can't run on macOS is refused. Build for this Mac and Install to Mac… refuse a tweak that needs an iOS framework macOS doesn't have, naming the tweak and the framework. A framework the app itself links only gets a warning. A tweak's own frameworks now get the stand-in Preferences framework too, as its libraries already did. The tooltips say that not every iPhone or iPad app runs under PlayCover, even without tweaks, and how to tell.

An iPad's page in the sidebar says iPad where it used to say phone. Check device on a LiveContainer app's pane looks on the device the app was last delivered to. It used to ask whichever device was connected and say the record still stood. Install to Mac… in Builds says why when the handover fails; it used to say nothing. Re-install… asks before it installs on a phone. The confirmation names the app, the build and the iPhone or iPad it goes to, and says so when that device isn't connected. Return re-installs, and Escape cancels. Graft no longer installs an update that needs a newer macOS than this Mac has. It says which macOS the update needs, offers no Try Again, and doesn't download it again at every launch; once the Mac is upgraded, the update goes ahead. When an update can't install itself, its message names the right download: Graft-Intel.zip on an Intel Mac, or on an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 13. The Builds list shows a build as soon as it ends, without relaunching Graft. A window opened behind another app lists the connected devices right away, instead of saying "Looking for devices…" until you switch to it. An iPhone or iPad newer than Graft's list of models shows its own name, or "iPad" or "iPhone", instead of its long device ID. Settings › Preflight shows "not connected" as information when no iPhone or iPad is plugged in, not as a failure. A build that installs still needs one. Edit, Remove, Stop building, Re-install, the Builds list and the build log use an app's display name, not its short name. The quit question names what's running: exporting an IPA, building an app, or building and installing one. The build log's header and the Builds list show a local date and time. A device's LiveContainer section no longer says it's managed by SideStore or AltStore when LiveContainer isn't installed. It says SideStore or AltStore is on the device, and to install or update LiveContainer with it. A get by version id downloads the build you picked when another build shares its version number. It used to take a staged copy of that number, which could be the other build. Every icon-only button has a VoiceOver name, such as "Update" or "Delete" plus the tweak's name. The Tweaks filter's placeholder fits its field. A device dump's output opens on its newest line. For people building Graft: the release check that the Intel build reads GraftBundleArch now reads Swift the way a Release build compiles it.

macOS 13 on Intel Macs. Graft-Intel.zip now runs on macOS 13 Ventura, as well as macOS 14 and later. It's still a test build. Graft.zip, for Apple silicon, still needs macOS 14. A Mac with Apple silicon on macOS 13 can run Graft-Intel.zip too, and its banner says Graft.zip needs macOS 14 or later. On macOS 13, the up and down arrow keys don't move through Add App's search results: click a result, or press Return to pick the first.

Get an older version… tells apart builds the App Store has under the same version number. They used to look like the same row twice. Now they read "1.2.0 (build 1 of 2)" and "1.2.0 (build 2 of 2)", numbered from the oldest, and hovering over one says which it is. Show More renumbers them when it finds an older one. Graft finds its own Python by name, whatever its version, as its updater already does. A later release built on a newer Python would otherwise skip the check that the app and its Python come from the same download, Apple silicon or Intel. For people building Graft: a release build runs the tests of Graft's ipatool patch and stops if one fails; each download is built for its own oldest macOS and checked against it; and an Intel release no longer passes its check when the app names GraftBundleArch only in a comment or an #if false block. The test suites also no longer depend on the Mac they run on, and a test build of the app keeps its settings apart from the Graft you use.

Intel Macs, as a test build. Graft-Intel.zip, beside Graft.zip on the release page, runs on an Intel Mac with macOS 14 or later. It stays a test build until it has run on a real Intel Mac. Everything works except what needs Apple silicon: App Store sign-in, getting and decrypting App Store apps (older versions and free ones included), and Build for this Mac with PlayCover. Those buttons are still there, disabled, with "Needs a Mac with Apple silicon". On an Intel Mac, use a decrypted IPA you already have, or dump one from a jailbroken device. App Store search still works, for adding an app by name, and needs no sign-in. Each download updates itself from its own zip, and checks that the update is the same build before installing it. If a release doesn't have your build's zip yet, Graft says there's no update for this Mac yet. Graft.zip opened on an Intel Mac says to download Graft-Intel.zip, with a button to the releases page. Graft-Intel.zip opened on an Apple silicon Mac runs, with a banner saying to download Graft.zip for everything. Help › Join the Graft Discord, the same button in Settings › Version, and a link in Graft › About Graft open the Graft Discord, for questions and help.

Get an older version… stops when the connection stalls. It used to wait about a minute on the version it was reading, mark that version as unavailable, and go on to the next one, up to a minute each. Now the list stops there and says reading that version timed out. The versions it had read are kept, so Try Again picks up where it stopped. If that version times out again, it's marked as unavailable and the list goes on. Get an older version… copes better with slow connections: a request for a version's details now fails only after 30 seconds with nothing arriving, not after 30 seconds in all. Export IPA… no longer freezes the window when it saves to a drive where it has to copy the file into place, such as some network and FAT drives. The window stays responsive while the file is copied, and Stop ends the copy and leaves nothing in the folder. If a file with the same name appears in the folder while the file is copied, Graft leaves it alone and says so. When an export fails, the error names the file you chose, not the temporary folder Graft built it in.

Get an older version. When a new version of an app breaks a tweak, Get an older version… on the app's pane lists the versions the App Store still has for your Apple ID, newest first, with their dates, and gets the one you pick. Graft then holds the app at that version: builds use it, and the pane says "Held at 1.2.0 · newest 1.4.0" instead of "update available", until you press Get latest from App Store. Only apps your Apple ID has, Apple doesn't serve every old version, and some apps refuse to run once they're too old. In Terminal: graft --appstore-versions --app <name>, then graft --appstore-get --app <name> --version-id <id>. A preferred version set in Edit App is now a hold too: the pane says "Held at", not "update available", and Get latest from App Store sets it back to latest. If PlayCover isn't installed, Build options on an app's pane now says so above Build for this Mac, with a Get PlayCover button that opens PlayCover's releases page on GitHub. Graft doesn't download or install PlayCover. When handing a build to PlayCover fails because it isn't installed, the error names that page too. Export IPA… in Build options saves the app's IPA with its tweaks injected, unsigned, where you choose, for an on-device signer or TrollStore on your own devices. Nothing is signed or sent to a device, whatever the app's delivery mode, and the export doesn't appear in Builds. In Terminal: graft example --export-ipa <file>.ipa, which checks it can write there before it builds. Under --json, a failed export's build-end says why in reason, such as exists or unwritable. Help › Star Graft on GitHub and Help › Support Graft on Ko-fi open those pages in your browser. The same two buttons are in Settings › Version, and Graft › About Graft links them too.

Help › Check for Updates… no longer offers Update for an update Graft is already downloading. It used to, and still said the update was available after the banner said it was ready. Now it says the download has started and the banner shows how it's going. For an update that's ready it offers Restart to Update, as the banner does, and after a failed try it says why, and offers Try Again when trying again can help. If you put an older Graft back after an update installed, Graft no longer says it couldn't update, as long as the copy you put back is 2.1 or later. It now checks the update log before it says an update failed. The log's times now include their offset from UTC.

Graft now updates itself. Automatic updates. When a newer Graft is out, Graft downloads it from GitHub in the background, checks it, and shows Restart to Update in the banner at the bottom of the window. If you don't restart, it installs the update when you quit. The old Graft.app goes to the Trash, so you can put it back. Checked before it's installed. The download must match the SHA-256 GitHub lists for it, and the app inside must be Graft, newer than yours, signed with the same developer's Developer ID as yours and notarized by Apple. If any check fails, Graft deletes the download and the banner links to the release page. Never in the middle of work. Graft doesn't install an update while it's building, installing or downloading an app. It waits until that's done, or until you quit. Settings › Updates has a second switch, Download and install updates automatically, on by default. With it off, the banner offers Update, which downloads, checks and restarts when you choose it. The first switch is now called Check for updates automatically. When it can't. Graft can't replace itself when it runs straight from Downloads, or from a folder your account can't change. The banner says so and links to the release page. If an install fails after Graft quits, Graft keeps the version you have, says so the next time it opens, and writes what happened to ~/Library/Logs/Graft/update.log. graft --download-update downloads and checks a newer Graft from Terminal. What Graft connects to lists the download. Remove Graft's Data. Help › Remove Graft's Data… lists everything Graft keeps outside Graft.app, each with its size and what it is: its folders, your App Store sign-in, ipatool's App Store components, the decryption model, your .p12 and SSH passwords, the graft link for Terminal, the app's own settings, the update log, and temporary files a stopped run left behind. Check what to remove, and it removes that and nothing else. Your passwords stay unless you check them, and anything config.yaml points to outside Graft's folders is never removed. It waits while Graft is building or downloading, and when it's done it says what it removed, so you can quit Graft and move it to the Trash. In Terminal, graft --remove-data lists the same, and --items removes what you name. Removing Graft has the whole list.

If Apple stops serving the macOS restore image that the bundled ipatool takes the App Store's frameworks from, the first sign-in or App Store action on a Mac now says so in plain words: a newer Graft fixes it, and the update notice (or Help › Check for Updates…) says when one is out. It used to show only ipatool's own error, such as "server returned 403 Forbidden". A Mac that already has those frameworks in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool isn't affected. Get (free) no longer adds an app to an Apple ID the question didn't name. If you signed in as someone else in Terminal while "Get … for free?" was open, the app went into that Apple ID's purchases. Graft now checks again as it gets the app, and if the Apple ID changed it says so and buys nothing. The question also no longer opens by itself when you come back to an app you left while Graft was checking. If you've made a keychain other than login your default in Keychain Access, Graft no longer reads only the login keychain to tell whether it's locked. With that default keychain locked, the App Store sign-in could ask for its password. Check again, in Settings and on the setup screen, and Preflight's Re-run say when Graft asked your shell less than 10 seconds before and used that answer, instead of looking as if they had asked again. Setting the Mac's clock back no longer holds them off. A login shell from Homebrew no longer costs Graft your shell's settings the first time it runs. macOS checks a new program before it starts it, which can take seconds on a slow network, and that time counted against the five seconds Graft gives your shell. A push into LiveContainer that the phone stopped answering, or that you stopped, just as the old copy was moved aside no longer leaves the app missing from LiveContainer's Documents. The old copy is put back. A phone that goes silent while Graft connects to it, lists its apps, or reads or writes LiveContainer's files is given up on after a minute, instead of waiting until you press Stop. An app that uses its developer's iCloud container now gets the "will probably crash at launch" warning when your profile has iCloud but not that container. A .p12, profile or App Store Connect key your user can't read (one copied with sudo belongs to root) gets a hint about its owner and permissions, not the Privacy & Security one. That hint now names Terminal too, for graft run there. A paid account setup that failed, then was stopped while it put things back, still says why it failed. A pipx graft whose appstore.ipatool names Graft.app's own ipatool no longer deletes Graft.app's App Store sign-in when it signs in. Neither does Graft.app when the setting spells that path another way: in another case, through a hard link, or under /System/Volumes/Data. When macOS's Keychain refuses a pipx graft's own ipatool, the hint says to sign in again with it in Terminal. It sent you to Graft.app, whose sign-in doesn't help that ipatool. Set Up Decryption's check for the App Store state passes over a folder that is a link, and Cancel and the time limit stop it like the rest of the step. Another user of this Mac could put a link in place of that state's folder in the Mac's Shared folder, to a network folder that is slow to answer, and the check, which runs as root, could keep waiting on it past Cancel and the time limit. It never read or changed anything there. Release Page on the update banner, and Open Release Page after Help › Check for Updates…, now open only Graft's own page for the version on offer. Graft keeps the last update check's answer between launches, and another program on your Mac could change it so the button opened a page somewhere else. Graft now builds the link from the version number, and drops a saved answer whose version isn't one. graft --check-update also names only that release's page, or Graft's latest release. Quit Anyway no longer leaves a stopped command running after Graft has gone. Graft gives a stopped command 10 seconds to clean up before it ends it outright, but Quit Anyway waited only 5, so a slow one, and the tools it had started, could run on without Graft. Quit Anyway now waits up to 13 seconds, and Graft still quits as soon as the work has stopped. Quitting while Graft sets up your signing account or removes its data now says Graft can't stop that partway and will quit when it finishes, and Quit Anyway does just that. It used to say Quit Anyway would stop it, then quit after 5 seconds and leave it running. Quitting while Graft checks your signing files stops the check, as Cancel does.

Graft now tells you when a new version is out, and has a new icon. Update notice. Once a day while it's open, Graft asks GitHub whether a newer version is out, through its own CLI (graft --check-update), and shows a banner if there is one. That's one request, sent as User-Agent: Graft, with nothing that identifies you or your Mac, and it never downloads or installs anything. Help › Check for Updates… asks any time, and Settings › Updates turns the daily check off. What Graft connects to lists it. What's New. Help › What's New… shows this changelog inside the app. A new icon: two pieces joined on the diagonal and taped, with a leaf at the tip. Get Again. When the version the App Store has is the one already staged, Get latest from App Store downloads nothing and says "Already have <version>". Get Again, or --again with --appstore-get, downloads it anyway.

Set Up Decryption suggests opening the app you picked first, with a button that does it: macOS sometimes clears the App Store state that step reads, even for an app you've already opened, and opening the app writes it again. If the state still isn't there, root stops before it copies or changes anything (the script exits 69) and the sheet says which app to open. The time limit root works under no longer measures an app through a link. Quitting, logging out or restarting while Graft is working (a build or install, an App Store download, setting up decryption or your signing account, a LiveContainer change, or a decrypt from a device) asks first. Keep Working cancels the quit; Quit Anyway stops the work cleanly, then quits. Installing LiveContainer waits up to 15 minutes for you to close LiveContainer only when it's updating a copy already on the device. A first install keeps the usual minute and the dropped-connection hint.

Graft no longer needs Terminal. Download it, open it, set it up in the app. Graft.app carries its own graft CLI, with its own Python, and every tool it uses: cyan, zsign, ldid, ipatool, UnfairPlay and the rest. There's no Homebrew, pipx, Python, Go, Xcode or libimobiledevice to install, except libimobiledevice for decrypting on a jailbroken device. Sign in to the App Store in the app. Settings › App Store › Sign In… takes your Apple ID, your password and, if Apple asks for one, the code it sends to your devices. They go only to Apple, through the ipatool inside Graft.app, and Graft saves none of them. Get (free). When your Apple ID doesn't have an app yet and it's free, Get latest from App Store in the app's Source IPA section becomes Get (free). It asks first, then adds the app to your purchases at no cost and downloads it. A paid app shows Open in App Store instead; Graft never buys anything. Setup, decryption and account changes happen in the app. The first run asks whether you have a paid Apple Developer account. With one, you choose your .p12 and profile and see the team and devices before Graft sets anything up. Settings › App Store › Set Up Decryption… enrolls this Mac for App Store decryption, behind macOS's administrator prompt. Graft explains the step first and never sees the password. Set Up Again… redoes it after you change Apple ID. Settings switches between a free Apple ID and a paid account, and replaces a paid account's certificate and profile when they expire, keeping your apps, repos and settings. App Store search. Add App opens on Search: type an app's name, pick it, and add it. No URL to paste, and no Apple ID needed to search. macOS 14 or later. Graft.app now opens on macOS 14 Sonoma as well as later versions. Graft 2.0 needs a Mac with Apple silicon. Graft 1.1 may work on an Intel Mac running macOS 15 or later, but it was never tested there. Graft 1.1 needs macOS 15; Going back to 1.1 installs its CLI with @v1.1.

Settings › Command-line tool › Install graft for Terminal links the app's own graft into ~/.local/bin, so the command updates with the app. Each app remembers the App Store it came from, and is checked for updates, its icon and its price there. Add App's Search has a Store picker, and Edit App can change an app's store. The App Store Connect key is set in Settings, and "Create the provisioning profile automatically" is in each app's Edit sheet. Builds has "Clean up old builds…", which applies your archive setting now. A decrypt UnfairPlay can't verify offers "Use it anyway…", which says what that risks first. Builds for this Mac under PlayCover no longer need Xcode: Graft.app carries the stand-in framework some tweaks need. Before zsign signs an app, Graft warns when its profile can't grant what the app asks for (App Groups, iCloud, push and the like), and says which are likely to crash it. A phone that has never trusted this Mac is told to tap Trust, and Graft waits a minute for it, instead of failing. Settings shows the version of the app and of the CLI it runs. Help › Licenses lists every bundled component, and each release page carries the source archive.

Re-saving a password no longer asks for your keychain password. In 1.1, storing a .p12 or SSH password over one already there asked for your login keychain password, and replaced it even when you canceled. The three known issues in 1.1 are fixed: renaming an app's bundle id removes its Apple Watch app, which can't follow it, so the install no longer fails; builds with a paid account no longer print a "PKCS#12 … BER" warning; cyan's color codes no longer show in the build log. A Stop during a sideload install ends promptly, and removes the IPA it staged on the phone. A phone that goes silent during an upload or an install is given up on after a minute, with a plain message, instead of hanging. A pulled cable gets a plain message too. Installing LiveContainer itself (--lc-install) is the exception: once Graft has asked you to close LiveContainer on the device, it waits up to 15 minutes for that. A push into LiveContainer lands whole or not at all. A cut-off push leaves nothing under the app's name, and the next push or Clean up removes what it left. Automatic provisioning puts every enabled iPhone and iPad in the profile, not the first three. A cached profile is reused only if it lists your current certificate and team, and Graft checks the key's team before it changes anything at Apple. Setting an App Store Connect key no longer rewrites the rest of the app_store_connect: section. An archive left by a failed install no longer takes a keep slot from a build you can re-install, and a clean-up never moves an archive a build is about to deliver. A failed paid setup, or a failed certificate replace, puts every file and password back as it was. A locked or unanswering login keychain gives a plain message after a minute, instead of hanging. The decryption check reads every binary itself, fat64 ones included, and never counts one it can't read as decrypted. App Store links with no app name in them, geo.itunes.apple.com links and itms-apps:// links are accepted, and older itunes.apple.com/gb/... links keep their store. Warnings from saving an app's options or an App Store Connect key show in the app instead of being lost.

Graft.app always runs the CLI inside it, never a graft installed with pipx. The pipx install still works on its own, with the tools you install. In config.yaml, an appstore.ipatool or appstore.unfairplay equal to 1.x's default counts as not set, so Graft.app's own copy runs, and so does one that isn't there any more, with a note in --appstore-status. A relative path there, or in appstore.unfairplay_models, is now ignored with a warning and read as not set. 1.x resolved it against the folder the CLI started in. An app with no store is looked up in the store of this Mac's region, then in the US store. 1.x asked only the US store. Signing in to the App Store in Graft replaces a sign-in your own ipatool made under 1.x. Your own ipatool then needs to sign in again if you use it in Terminal. The CLI no longer installs frida. Decrypting on a jailbroken device uses frida-ios-dump's own. The Graft.app download is an aggregate of separate programs, each under its own license. The CLI inside it is distributed under GPL-3.0-or-later, and Graft's own source code stays MIT. Coming from 1.x: Upgrading from Graft 1.x covers your config, your pipx graft, the Homebrew tools you no longer need, your App Store sign-in, and going back to 1.1. Staying on 1.1? Pin its CLI to @v1.1 before any pipx upgrade or pipx reinstall, or they bring in 2.0's: see Going back to 1.1. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's App Store components (about 320 MB, skipped if a 1.x ipatool already downloaded them) from Apple and its Unicorn emulator from PyPI, and can take several minutes. What Graft connects to lists every host.

Graft works with a free Apple ID. With a free Apple ID, Graft builds the tweaked IPA unsigned and pushes it into LiveContainer, which signs it when you import it. You need LiveContainer on the device, installed with SideStore, AltStore, iloader or Impactor. graft --init asks which kind of account you have, and switching to a paid account later keeps your apps, repos and settings. The Mac app's setup screen lists every missing tool with its install command, and missing tools show as a notice instead of a failed build. Finding your iPhone or iPad no longer needs libimobiledevice. An app can be pinned to one LiveContainer when the device has several. graft --lc-clean removes only files Graft pushed, and Graft won't overwrite a file in LiveContainer's Documents unless it knows the file is its own. --dry-run previews only a build and --prune-builds. Any other command refuses it instead of running for real. A stopped build shows as Stopped, adds nothing to Builds and leaves no temporary files behind. Your Apple ID data is removed from every IPA Graft builds or installs. Your .p12 and SSH passwords no longer show in process listings, and Graft's folders and files are readable only by your user account. The Mac app picks up changes made in Terminal when you come back to its window, and says so when config.yaml can't be read. A locked phone is asked to unlock, instead of reporting "no LiveContainer found". The app works with csh and tcsh, or a shell that forces color, and no longer hangs on a slow shell startup file. For scripts, --json output is pure JSON for every command, and LiveContainer errors have their own exit code, 21. Known issues, fixed in 2.0: a renamed bundle id failed on apps with an Apple Watch app; paid builds printed a "PKCS#12 … BER" warning; some cyan lines showed raw color codes in the app's build log. On 2026-11-19 the 1.1 download was rebuilt without the build machine's file paths and code-coverage data. Same version, no other changes.

The first public release: the graft CLI, installed with pipx, and Graft.app, which runs it. A paid Apple Developer account was required. Injects .deb and .dylib tweaks into a decrypted IPA with cyan, and delivers it into LiveContainer, keeping its bundle id, or signs it with zsign and installs it as a normal app. Gets the source IPA three ways: an IPA you have, a dump from your own jailbroken device (frida-ios-dump or bagbak), or the App Store with your Apple ID, through ipatool and UnfairPlay. Finds tweaks on canister.me and in APT repositories, and checks them for updates. Keeps a build history, archived builds per app version for rollback, and a delivery state that says when a device is behind your config. Installs, updates and signs LiveContainer itself, including side-by-side instances, and makes per-app profiles through App Store Connect. Runs builds on this Mac under PlayCover. Needed macOS 15 or later, Python 3.11 or later, and tools from Homebrew and the Xcode Command Line Tools.

Common symptoms and error messages, and their likely cause. Symptom Likely cause ApplicationVerificationFailed The .p12 and profile are from different teams, or the device's UDID isn't in the profile. MismatchedApplicationIdentifierEntitlement The profile doesn't allow this bundle id; use a wildcard profile. Installing LiveContainer: delete an old zsign-signed copy on the device first. DeviceLocked Unlock the device. Developer Mode is off on <device> The device runs iOS 16 or later with Developer Mode off, and the app is signed with a development profile, so it wouldn't open. Turn it on in Settings › Privacy & Security › Developer Mode (a real build has made the switch appear), then confirm after the device restarts. An app, such as an emulator, says it needs JIT Graft doesn't turn on JIT. StikDebug, an app on the iPhone, does. On iOS 26 and recent iPhones, only apps built to support it can get JIT, whatever tool you use. wrong password from zsign The .p12 password is wrong. Library not loaded: @rpath/libexample.dylib Add a copy of that library to the app's tweaks; see Shared libraries. couldn't extract some-tweak.deb The download is probably an HTML error page; fetch it again. A guest app in LiveContainer doesn't remember its login LiveContainer was signed with a wildcard profile's entitlements (for example by zsign). Reinstall it from Graft with a paid account. A dump from a jailbroken device times out Check the device's Decrypt card. The bundled ipatool takes the App Store's frameworks from one macOS restore image, at a fixed Apple address, and checks every file it takes against its source's pins, so no other image can stand in. If Apple removes that file, a Mac that hasn't downloaded them yet can't get them; Apple's server then answers "403 Forbidden" (or "404 Not Found"), which the error's details show. What Graft keeps outside the app, and how to remove it from the Help menu or in Terminal. Dragging Graft.app to the Trash removes the app and everything inside it. What it made outside the app stays until you remove it.

Help › Remove Graft's Data… lists all of it, with sizes. Check what to remove, then press Remove…. It waits while Graft is building, installing, downloading or setting something up. When it's done, it says what it removed: quit Graft, then move Graft.app to the Trash. Removing can't be undone.

graft --remove-data # list it all, with sizes; removes nothing graft --remove-data --items all --dry-run # what --items all would remove graft --remove-data --items all # every item marked "removed with all" graft --remove-data --items all,passwords # and your passwords graft --remove-data --items cache,temp # only these

You can build Graft.app from the repository with xcodegen and Xcode, and run its tests there. brew install xcodegen cd Graft && xcodegen generate open Graft.xcodeproj Or from the command line: xcodebuild -project Graft/Graft.xcodeproj -scheme Graft -configuration Debug \ -destination 'platform=macOS' build Build Debug: it runs the graft it finds on your PATH, and its setup screen first shows the commands that install the CLI, each with a Copy button. Release builds come from scripts/graft-release, below. A plain Xcode Release build has no CLI inside it, so it opens on a screen saying so. Tests: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev]' .venv/bin/python -m pytest cd Graft && TEST_RUNNER_PATH="$PWD/../.venv/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" \ xcodebuild test -scheme Graft -destination 'platform=macOS' The app is SwiftUI. It runs the graft CLI as a subprocess for every action and reads its --json events. Both share config.yaml and log.sqlite, and there's no daemon. A release build carries the CLI and its own Python inside the app. A build from Xcode runs the CLI it finds on your PATH, such as the repo's venv. scripts/graft-release builds the distributable app: everything bundled for one processor (Graft.zip for Apple silicon, Graft-Intel.zip for Intel Macs, with --arch x86_64), with a universal app executable in both, so Graft.zip opened on an Intel Mac shows a screen that names Graft-Intel.zip. Each is built for its own oldest macOS, 14.0 for Graft.zip and 13.0 for Graft-Intel.zip. It's signed with a Developer ID identity and zipped. Then scripts/verify-bundle (with --arch x86_64 for the Intel build) checks the sealed app, including that no program in it needs a newer macOS than that. See Graft/README.md, and docs/network.md for every host Graft and its tools contact, including what a release build downloads.
